Industry News: Warhol’s Watches

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1792 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Piaget’s second collaboration with The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts translates the pop artist’s 1986 Camouflage self-portraits into dials made of gemstone marquetry.
  • Recent findings suggest that one brand, however, stood out.
  • Housed in an 18-karat gold, 45 mm cushion-shaped case designed by Jean-Claude Gueit, Piaget’s then artistic director, the striking piece, which was part of a limited series manufactured between 1972 and 1977, featured a black onyx dial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Piaget’s second collaboration with The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts translates the pop artist’s 1986 Camouflage self-portraits into dials made of gemstone marquetry.

Recent findings suggest that one brand, however, stood out. Warhol owned at least seven wristwatches by the Swiss maison, Piaget. Founded in 1874 in La Côte-aux-Fées, a village in the heart of Switzerland’s Jura mountain range, the house was renowned in the latter half of the 20th century for its creative selection of timepieces in unusual shapes, many featuring dials made of exotic ornamental stones. One of those watches, a quartz-powered reference 15102 model that Warhol purchased from the brand in 1973, now forms the foundation for a Piaget collection bound to appeal to lovers of art in general and fans of Warhol’s revolutionary oeuvre in particular.

Housed in an 18-karat gold, 45 mm cushion-shaped case designed by Jean-Claude Gueit, Piaget’s then artistic director, the striking piece, which was part of a limited series manufactured between 1972 and 1977, featured a black onyx dial. Fittingly, it was called the Black Tie. In 1988, Piaget purchased Warhol’s watch at Sotheby’s landmark sale.

Recent findings suggest that the artist’s choice of Piaget was no accident. In the 1950s and ’60s, the house had built its reputation on extreme thinness, introducing ultra-thin movements that transformed the watches into slim, supple pieces of jewelry. By the 1960s, Piaget had paired that technical prowess with a bolder sensibility: gold bracelets, vivid hardstone dials, and silhouettes that owed more to the jeweler’s bench than to the watchmaker’s. The result was a crossover brand that suited the decade’s appetite for spectacle. For Warhol, who drew no line between commerce and art, a watch that doubled as a gem-set object was irresistible. The Black Tie’s onyx dial, as sleek and dark as a lacquered cigarette case, could not have been better suited to the man who documented the era’s elite so closely.

Twenty-six years after Piaget purchased the Black Tie, the brand used the occasion of its 140th anniversary in 2014 to create a revival collection called Black Tie Vintage. The line caused such a stir among Piaget’s clientele that in 2024, for its sesquicentennial, the maison decided to up the ante. Thanks to a collaboration with The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, Piaget was given the rights to rename the Black Tie Vintage watch after Warhol himself.

Recent findings suggest that the first collaborative watch to emerge from Piaget’s work with the foundation was the 2025 Collage, a limited edition of 50 pieces featuring an artful composition of ornamental stones—yellow Namibian serpentine, pink opal, and green chrysoprase—inspired by Warhol’s Polaroids. This month, Piaget has introduced a second piece, which also uses ornamental stone marquetry, this time to pay tribute to the Camouflage self-portraits that Warhol created in 1986.

“When you buy it, you don’t only buy a watch, you buy a whole story and heritage,” Jean-Bernard Forot, Piaget’s head of patrimony, tells ARTnews. “You can, of course, talk about the material, what it does for you. But at the same time, you have to talk about Warhol, you have to talk about Piaget, you have to talk about art.”.

Limited to 86 pieces, after the year in which Warhol created the eight-print Camouflage series, the watch, whose dial combines the ornamental stones sodalite and turquoise with satin-finished yellow gold and polished rose gold, faithfully interprets the artist’s work without blindly mimicking it.

“Camouflage is very difficult to work on, even in design, because we don’t just copy and paste the artwork—we have to find another way to express camouflage,” Forot states.

In a recent development, among the final serial group of paintings Warhol completed before his untimely death in 1987, the works paid homage to the military-inspired camouflage pattern, originally intended to help soldiers blend in with their surroundings. In Warhol’s hands, they became a comment on Abstract Expressionism, not to mention a deeply personal statement on his lifelong effort to conceal his true self beneath wigs, makeup, and a carefully constructed facade.

According to recent reports, printed in acid brights across enormous canvases, the swirling forms feature in self-portraits overlayed with Warhol’s face, framed by his signature shock of hair. For an artist who spent his life hiding in plain sight, the Camouflage series is arguably his most meta work.

Sources indicate that in order to capture the essence of the paintings on the face of a watch, Piaget’s artisans took some liberties with color. Rather than emphasizing Warhol’s use of yellow, for example, they highlighted the brand’s use of turquoise, Forot says.

“Once the team finished the drawing, which was validated by The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, then they started working with the gem material,” he states. “We have to try to remain true to both the design itself as well as the techniques.”.

Recent findings suggest that study the dial of the watch and you’ll see something of an optical illusion: a sense of depth and texture that isn’t quite there. “When you look at the Piaget Camouflage, you have the feeling that you have four layers,” Forot states. “But in fact, it’s an illusion because they are all flat and on the same level. Even if you have the feeling that the turquoise is above the gold, in fact, it’s at the same level.”.

Industry observers note that the careful craftsmanship required to make the watch—each dial features 27 pieces of gold and ornamental stone marquetry and takes more than 100 hours of labor to design, research, and craft—is a testament to Piaget’s decades of expertise in the esoteric world of gem-setting. Since the maison introduced gold and color into its watches in the 1960s, it has worked with some 50 different ornamental stones, including lapis lazuli, jade, coral, onyx, and tiger’s eye.

The maison’s legitimacy in the realm of color is unassailable—and enduring. Piaget designated 2026 its “Year of Color,” based on its Colours of Extraleganza collection, representing the third and final chapter of a high jewelry trilogy that began with the maison’s 150th anniversary in 2024. “Piaget is really coming back to visibility in color and gold,” Forot states.

It has been revealed that while the blend of hues on the dial of the Camouflage watch lends the piece its name and raison d’être, don’t overlook its iconic gold frame nor the movement that ticks within. The cushion-shaped case features three rows of textured grooves known as gadroons, a Piaget signature. It houses a self-winding manufacture movement, the 501 P1. And let’s not forget the caseback, where Andy Warhol’s signature appears alongside the number of timepieces in the limited series.

Best of all, the Camouflage limited edition, like the Collage that came before it, is steeped in the lore that swirls around Warhol’s personal history with Piaget.

It has been revealed that “Warhol was a real collector—of everything,” Forot says. “But even if he owned many watches from many brands—including Patek Philippe, Cartier, Bulgari, and so on—there is only one picture with him and the founder of a watchmaking organization. And it’s Yves Piaget.”.

It has been revealed that the legendary chairman of the maison, Yves Piaget is the fourth generation of his family to be involved in the business, which was founded by Georges-Édouard Piaget in 1874 and acquired by the Swiss luxury group Richemont in 1988. In the 1970s, at the height of the brand’s 20th-century popularity, Yves and Warhol became friends.

A photo of the men dated 1979 offers proof that they found common ground in their shared love of timepieces. At the time, Yves presided over the Piaget Society, a glamorous social circle centered on the brand and its community of jet-setting movers and shakers. And Warhol, of course, had the Factory, his studio in Manhattan, a hub of art, filmmaking, and creativity.

“They weren’t exactly the same, but they were both surrounded by artists, extravagant personalities—they were social long before The Social Network,” Forot says. “In a sense, they had the same philosophy.”.

Yves’ recollections of Warhol during that time paint the artist as a quiet figure, whose later fame didn’t square with his penchant for careful observation.

Nevertheless, the two hit it off. Yves invited Warhol to Palm Beach to attend the world cup of polo, a sport that the maison made famous through its 1979 Polo timepiece, an emblem of the rich and famous. And he continued to send Warhol gifts, including boxes of chocolate, that the artist, a true magpie, kept as part of his time capsules. Stored in cardboard boxes, the objects, ephemera, letters, and gifts Warhol collected included personal relics from his multiyear friendship with Yves, although Forot jokes that the box of chocolate, while part of the collection housed by The Andy Warhol Museum in Pittsburgh, is, thankfully, empty.

According to recent reports, warhol’s attraction to the brand was hardly anomalous. Piaget’s clientele included more than its fair share of the rich and famous, including Jackie O, Elizabeth Taylor, and Halston. Even Salvador Dalí was a longtime collaborator. In 1967 the surrealist teamed with Piaget on a collaborative collection of gold watches and jewelry, long before such partnerships became commonplace. Featuring gold coins, dubbed Dali D’Or, emblazoned with profile portraits of himself and his wife, Gala, the watches and jewels that emerged from the partnership offer yet another testament to Piaget’s high-flying reputation as the watch for those in the know and a symbol of wealth, taste, and extravagance, all qualities that continue to define the brand today.

Michael Dayton Hermann, managing director of strategic initiatives at The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, notes that the collaboration with Piaget “is an expression of how the artist’s vision remains as relevant and compelling today as ever.”.

In a recent development, “This unique ongoing project is especially meaningful given Warhol’s personal friendship with Yves Piaget and his passion for the maison’s watches, which he collected during his lifetime,” Hermann tells ARTnews. “It also embodies Warhol’s belief in the creative possibilities of art and commerce, generating proceeds that support the foundation’s philanthropic mission, which has awarded more than $300 million in grants to advance contemporary visual art.”.

Just as the collaboration celebrates Warhol’s singular take on the role art plays in commerce, it equally underscores Piaget’s decades-old legitimacy in the world of art. Watches may not be the first things that come to mind when recalling Warhol and his legacy, but he collected them, wore them, and, in the case of Piaget, befriended the man who made them. Think of the Camouflage limited edition less as a commercial arrangement and more as the next chapter of a decades-long conversation started by Warhol and carried on in gold and gems.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The new London Museum has been a humongous undertaking: 10 years in the making, costing £437 million in total against a budget of £337 million, and yet, after all that time and money, it’s hard to know where any of it went.
  • Sources indicate that from 1976 to 2022, the city’s museum, then called the Museum of London, occupied a site on London Wall at next to the Barbican complex.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The new London Museum has been a humongous undertaking: 10 years in the making, costing £437 million in total against a budget of £337 million, and yet, after all that time and money, it’s hard to know where any of it went.

Sources indicate that from 1976 to 2022, the city’s museum, then called the Museum of London, occupied a site on London Wall at next to the Barbican complex. It moved to Farringdon, a grittier neighbor of the City’s financial district, because the old building was hard for visitors to find and too small to display the full collection. Related Articles Bloomberg Donates 14,000 Artifacts Unearthed in Renovation to London Museum Warhol's Watches.

In a recent development, the latest space is bright and airy, closer to an Erewhon café than a museum lobby. An on-site café, open around the clock from Thursday to Sunday, serves hot chocolate and ginger beer. The furnishings, though, feel random in such a pristine setting: a flock of large plastic sheep meant for sitting on, and shop signs from London fixtures like the Odeon cinema and Morley’s, the fried chicken chain. When was the last time any Londoner saw a sheep in the city? In theory, all of this should appeal to Londoners who have taken up early-morning run clubs, traded pints for matcha lattes and aren’t above a gimmicky bit of decor.

“People are looking for community, and they will have it in the museum,” Sharon Ament, the museum’s director, told ARTnews.

The architects, Asif Khan and Stanton Williams, working with the conservation specialists Julian Harrap Architects, have designed a space that’s inviting.

“It took people until the 21st century to realize that cultural institutions are for everyone, and that’s what we strive to make here,” Khan told ARTnews at the press preview. He wants visitors to dip in and out of the story of London without feeling as if they’re in a museum. “When we look at audiences outside of the regular museum visitors, many find it challenging and don’t feel welcome. This is a welcome for those people,” Khan said. Entry is free, there are three separate entrances, and built-in sofas with reading lights invite passersby to stop in, though few people pass through Farringdon unless they’re waiting for the nightclub Fabric or the cocktail bar Space Talk to open.

Sources indicate that still, London is a city of 9.1 million people and a global center for art, film, music, finance and fashion. Finding stories that capture its quirks shouldn’t be that hard.

Industry observers note that the museum is divided into three sections. Real Time, at the main entrance, represents London today and includes Banksy’s Piranhas sentry box. (What could be more London than Banksy?) In the Linbury Hall, Our Time attempts to tie the city together through objects like the Lord Mayor’s State Coach from 1757, the Buckingham Palace switchboard and Syd’s Coffee Stall, an East End food cart that operated from 1919 to 2019. Downstairs is Past Time, perhaps the only part of the museum that feels like a museum. It’s the most educational section, with small rooms on the women’s suffrage movement and the Great Fire of London. The rest of the floor is scattered with a piece of a fatberg, Tom Daley’s diving trunks from the London 2012 Olympics, a chair owned by Charles Dickens, a 2,000-year-old Roman wall painting, Anna Pavlova’s tutu for The Dying Swan and more.

In a recent development, the London Museum is a work in progress and until it figures out what sets it apart from the city’s other museums, it will remain a large crèche, where parents can bring their children to roam freely. But there’s still some hope: in 2028, the museum will open two temporary exhibition spaces, perhaps the museum will finally lean into its London-ness and celebrate the cornerstones that makes the city so glamorous and gritty, from the Teddy Boys of 1950s, Mods and Rockers of the 1960s to the Sloane Rangers of the late 1970s and 1980s.

Until the London Museum gets it right, the city has the Bayeux Tapestry, on view at the British Museum through July 11, 2027, with tickets topping out at £33 ($44). At the preview, word went around that one journalist had skipped it in favor of the 950-year-old cloth. In hindsight, I should have done the same, or stayed home to play Grand Theft Auto VI.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti.
  • Industry observers note that A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck.
  • In a recent development, from a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti. If you’ve ever scrambled for scarves or turtlenecks, welcome to the kissing booth of knowledge! Join us as we navigate the lifecycle of hickeys, from their eye-catching start to their subtle fade, and learn how to speed up their departure.

Industry observers note that A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck. This intense suction causes the tiny blood vessels under the skin, a.k.a. capillaries, to burst and release blood into the surrounding tissues. The immediate result? An unmistakable red or purple mark that gradually shifts to a darker shade as it heals.

In a recent development, from a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing. They showcase the skin’s sensitivity and the body’s rapid response to minor vascular injury. Not so romantic when you think about it scientifically, right? But hey, it’s all part of the human experience of showing affection — or something like that.

When you get a hickey, your body starts a healing process that resembles how it deals with other bruises. Here’s a more detailed look at each stage of a hickey’s life cycle.

In a recent development, immediately after the passionate moment, a hickey appears on the skin, screaming in shades of bright red or deep purple. This initial coloration is due to blood from the ruptured capillaries pooling beneath the skin’s surface in response to the suction. It’s your skin’s way of signaling that there’s been some minor internal damage in that area.

As the hickey begins to heal, it undergoes a whole wardrobe of color transformations, showcasing your body’s metabolic process at work.

Recent findings suggest that initially, the hickey darkens as the blood begins to oxidize. Then, after a few days, the body starts to break down and reabsorb the blood, so it turns lighter — going from blue to green to brown and, finally, mellow yellow. This rainbow journey reflects the breakdown of hemoglobin, the iron-containing substance in the blood, into biliverdin and bilirubin.

It has been revealed that finally, your hickey starts to ghost you. Over a week or two, depending on factors like your skin type, overall health, how severe the hickey was., and how your body rides the healing waves, the last traces of your hickey fade into nothing.

During this stage, the body’s immune system clears away the remaining by-products of the broken-down blood. White blood cells swoop in like a cleanup crew at a festival, gobbling up and digesting the debris in a process called phagocytosis, while increased blood flow to the area helps to flush out the remnants.

Need a hickey gone yesterday? Here’s how to help your hickey heal. Start with a cold pack — grab a spoon from the freezer or a chilled gel pack and gently press it against your hickey. This will help reduce any swelling and scatter the blood pooling under your skin, which can help minimize that bold bruise.

Sources indicate that after using cold treatment for the first 48 hours, it’s time to turn up the heat. Switch to warm compresses to get the blood flowing smoothly again. A few minutes a few times a day invites more circulation to the hickey zone, helping you hustle through healing and clear out the blood remnants more swiftly.

Industry observers note that you can also try a dab of comfrey ointment. Research shows it may reduce bruise size and coloration for some peeps.

Caught off guard? A little concealer or foundation over the hickey makes it less noticeable.

In a recent development, not into makeup? Scarves and high-necked shirts are also great accessories for your camouflage arsenal.

Typically, a hickey will last anywhere from 5 days to 2 weeks, depending on its severity and your body’s healing capabilities.

Communication is key! Let your partner know your feelings about receiving a hickey — some might find it fun, while others may prefer to keep their necks clear.

While generally harmless, hickeys can sometimes lead to complications like skin infections or, very rarely, blood clots. It’s best to keep the affection gentle to avoid any complications.

Sources indicate that hickeys are nothing more than bruises in disguise. They start as bright red to purple love stamps and gradually fade over several days to a couple of weeks. Speed up the process with heat and cold packs or a splodge of comfrey cream.

Sources indicate that remember, the best approach to handling hickeys — like all aspects of relationships — is communication and care. So go forth, love responsibly, and keep a scarf handy, just in case!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The FBI is seeking a warrant to search electronic devices belonging to a Grand Rapids man accused of stealing art from two Michigan art museums.
  • In a recent development, according to a federal affidavit, Mikolai Augustine Stasiulewicz, 27, allegedly stole a color lithograph by artist Ellsworth Kelly, from Western Michigan University’s (WMU) Richmond Center for the Visual Arts on June 23.
  • It has been revealed that stasiulewicz is also alleged to have stolen a 16th-century Albrecht Dürer print from the Grand Rapids Art Museum (GRAM) on July 2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The FBI is seeking a warrant to search electronic devices belonging to a Grand Rapids man accused of stealing art from two Michigan art museums. The news was reported by multiple outlets, including MLive.

In a recent development, according to a federal affidavit, Mikolai Augustine Stasiulewicz, 27, allegedly stole a color lithograph by artist Ellsworth Kelly, from Western Michigan University’s (WMU) Richmond Center for the Visual Arts on June 23. A worker notified WMU police that the work was missing, and Stasiulewicz, who was caught on surveillance video carrying the framed print, was identified through facial-recognition analysis by Michigan State Police. Related Articles 13th-Century Carving Stolen by Art Thief 'Eric the Belgian' Recovered in the UK Stolen Picasso Prints Found Under Pile of Clothes in French Riviera Apartment.

It has been revealed that stasiulewicz is also alleged to have stolen a 16th-century Albrecht Dürer print from the Grand Rapids Art Museum (GRAM) on July 2. According to the FBI, he had been seen at the museum on June 17, “in what appeared to be a pre-theft surveillance visit.” Between the two thefts, he is accused of entering nonpublic areas at the Muskegon Museum of Art on June 25; however, Muskegon police remarked he didn’t take anything.

The FBI, which eventually took over the case, learned during its investigations that Stasiulewicz had met with a man on July 8 at the Gun Lake Casino Resort in Wayland, Michigan. Surveillance video shows him leaving with an unknown amount of cash.

Stasiulewicz was found dead in his home on July 30. According to the Kent County Medical Examiner’s Office, he died of a morphine overdose on July 26. Although the office’s autopsy report rules the death an accident, it also notes that “the decedent is currently under investigation by the FBI for involvement in an art gallery theft,” and that a brother had told police that may have played a part in his death.

Four artworks, including the Kelly, valued at $10,000 and the Dürer, valued at $10,000–$20,000, were found at the home the next day.

On Monday, November 23, the FBI sought a warrant to search Stasiulewicz’s cellphone and laptop computer to determine if any others were involved in the thefts. “In my training and experience, and that of the Art Crime Team, phones and computers like the devices will often be used to communicate with co-conspirators,” FBI Special Agent Evan Alkema wrote in the federal affidavit. “They may contain evidence of communications about what art pieces to steal, negotiations for sale prices, and arrangements to transfer and ‘fence’ the stolen works.”.

Since its inception in 2004, the FBI’s Art Crime Team, which handles cases involving the theft, forgery, and trafficking of art and cultural artifacts, has recovered more than 20,000 objects valued at $1 billion.

Stasiulewicz was an amateur artist who studied at the Interlochen Center of the Arts, the FBI said.

Tech Report: Atelier Manferdini uses digital glitches to shape tile-and-metal facade of Virginia power station

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (469 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Dave Huh unless stated.
  • California-based studio Atelier Manferdini has created an expressive facade system for an electrical substation in Virginia, USA, using metal and colourful tile to represent the flow of electrical power within.
  • Called InVisible, the project was carried out for Dominion Energy, an electricity provider that was updating the substation in Crystal City, Northern Virginia, just outside of Washington DC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Dave Huh unless stated.

California-based studio Atelier Manferdini has created an expressive facade system for an electrical substation in Virginia, USA, using metal and colourful tile to represent the flow of electrical power within.

Called InVisible, the project was carried out for Dominion Energy, an electricity provider that was updating the substation in Crystal City, Northern Virginia, just outside of Washington DC.

Atelier Manferdini founder Elena Manferdini, who is Italian and teaches at Sci-Arc in Los Angeles, mentioned that her studio sought to translate the largely functional structure into something more human.

“Critical infrastructure is essential to our cities, yet the Dominion Energy substation is fundamentally designed for machines rather than people,” Manferdini told Dezeen.

“With inVisible, we wanted to explore this dichotomy, transforming a purely functional structure into something meaningful to the surrounding community,” she continued.

“While the interior responds to the needs of machines, the exterior becomes an opportunity to engage with people through color, pattern, and perception, creating a dialogue between infrastructure and the human scale of the city.”.

The substation converts power into different voltages to facilitate the transmission of energy, and the patterns on the sculptural facade were computationally designed to represent that process.

Atelier Manferdini used programming site Processing, which came out of the MIT Media Lab in the early 2000s, to design the colourful tile band that lines the bottom of the structure.

This pattern incorporates 10 colours and tiles of three different sizes, two, four, and six inches across – a reference to voltages – along with “glitches” in the program to create the graphic.

It recalls the Boogie Woogie works of modernist artist Piet Mondrian, which were based on the rhythms of cities.

Above the ceramic pattern, the studio placed massive gridded aluminium panels.

The panels create a ventilated facade system, set at different distances from the exterior walls and stacked where they meet so that sunlight passes through different densities in the gridded pattern, creating a variable light effect.

“The folds catch light and cast shadows, allowing the surface to shift with the time of day and the viewer’s position,” said the studio.

At night, the panels are backlit by programmable LEDs.

Overall, the studio remarked that it considers the contrast between the monochromatic metal and colour tile patterns a unified image.

“Quiet and metallic above, saturated and granular below, the two bands form a unified architectural composition,” said the studio, with the unseen machines humming with electricity inside.

Other creative takes on infrastructure include a power station in China that Schmidt Hammer Lassen shrouded with steel lamellas and topped with a walkway, as well as a sculptural stormwater facility in Toronto by GH3, a Canadian studio well known for its aesthetic treatment of otherwise overlooked infrastructure.

Photography by Dave Huh unless stated.

  • If you’re caught without bug bite cream or ointment, don’t worry — plenty of simple home remedies can provide quick relief.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wondering how to get rid of mosquito bites overnight? Discover simple home remedies for quick relief. From crushed ice to aloe vera, explore easy solutions to soothe itching and inflammation for a peaceful night’s sleep.

If you’re caught without bug bite cream or ointment, don’t worry — plenty of simple home remedies can provide quick relief. From soothing aloe vera to the calming effects of oatmeal, discover easy solutions to alleviate itching and inflammation so you can sleep peacefully.

Just as you’d ice an injury, icing a bug bite can help decrease inflammation and temporarily numb the pain.

If icy cold treatments aren’t your vibe, you can apply heat instead to soothe your bump.

Aloe vera gel does more than soothe sunburns! It can also help ease bug bites and help them heal.

Recent findings suggest that baking soda can remove the itch. To make a paste, mix 1 tablespoon of it with a splash of water (not too much). Apply it to your bite as you would zit cream. Keep it on for 10 minutes before rinsing it off.

Recent findings suggest that did you know basil (yes, like the kind in your pasta) has a rich history as a skin infection remedy? It contains antioxidants that may bring down bug bite inflammation.

Industry observers note that to whip up your own basil rub, boil a couple cups of water with 1/2 ounce of dried basil leaves. Cool the mixture before applying it to a washcloth and gently massaging it onto the bite for sweet relief.

You already know apple cider vinegar (fermented liquid from apples) is a huge player in the natural remedy world.

Some people use it to clean due to its antimicrobial effects, and others mix it into food or drinks for its possible health benefits (like helping with blood sugar issues).

Its beauty with bites is that it can help ease burning or stinging while disinfecting your scratchy little bump.

Onion juice (while not delicious) has antifungal and antibacterial properties, which could possibly help ward off infection. Plus, it could make your bite sting less. Just dab a bit of raw onion juice onto your bites. The downside? We’re not sure how well it works … and it’s kinda stinky.

Thyme has been used to help with skin concerns for a long time. You can use it to help decrease irritation by chopping it up and applying the teeny leaves directly to your bite for 10 minutes. You can also boil thyme, soak a cloth in the cooled liquid, and wrap it around your bite.

Peppermint oil may work as an anti-itch agent. Mix it with carrier oil (like olive oil) before applying it to your skin, though!

Sources indicate that another natural anti-itcher and astringent, lemon balm, may be helpful. You can either apply a lemon balm cream or chop up the leaves and apply them right to the bite.

Recent findings suggest that witch hazel is a natural wonder with many uses for skin concerns such as acne and psoriasis. It can tackle inflammation and burning while helping your bug bite heal.

Sources indicate that this herb may work, but the science is a little dicey. On its own, arnica is toxic, so any over-the-counter products you find have been carefully diluted for your safety.

The yummy tea that calms and soothes at bedtime has many other uses, including potentially calming an irritated bug bite. Steep the tea bag for 20 minutes before squeezing it out and applying it to your bite once it’s cooled.

Blend minced garlic with petroleum jelly or fragrance-free lotion. Place the mixture on your bite for 10 minutes before removing it and applying a cool cloth.

Icing the bite for 10 minutes and then placing a mixture of baking soda and water on it for 10 minutes is a strong choice.

Industry observers note that though not tested for this purpose, some people turn to Vicks to soothe mosquito bites. It’s possible that its antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties could help heal and soothe mosquito bites. But FYI, this product isn’t considered the best defense against mosquito bites.

In a recent development, some toothpastes are cooling, so that sensation may offer temporary relief. Some people use toothpaste on insect bites since many toothpastes contain astringents, which can help shrink tissues.

Using repellent to prevent bug bites is a good idea. PSA: DEET and lemon eucalyptus oil are safe ways to repel insects.

Mosquitoes are low-key little monsters that cause the most insect bites worldwide. Most bites aren’t serious, but mosquitoes can potentially carry diseases.

Ointments, creams, or simple home remedies can help stop the pesky itch after bites. But remember that some natural substances can cause allergic reactions. That stated, it’s always a good idea to do a patch test first.

Cyberpunk 2's director just called GTA 6 "a technological and creative miracle"

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, GTA 6 has been out for less than a week, and it isn't just players and critics who are losing their minds.
  • The most dramatic reaction I've read came from Igor Sarzyński, creative director on Cyberpunk 2.
  • He joked that Cyberpunk 2 was cancelled and he was off to sweep leaves in his garden.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, GTA 6 has been out for less than a week, and it isn't just players and critics who are losing their minds. I gave it 5/5 in my GTA 6 review, and it holds a 99 Metascore, tying Ocarina of Time as the highest-rated game ever. As more people play and see more of Leonida, other game developers (those who really know what's what) are lining up to say they're a bit rattled.

The most dramatic reaction I've read came from Igor Sarzyński, creative director on Cyberpunk 2. Reported on Shift Delete, he posted on Bluesky on Saturday evening, two days after launch, and started with "GTA VI-induced-open-world-game-dev-depression is real", then called it "probably the single greatest artistic achievement in history" and "a technological and creative miracle".

He joked that Cyberpunk 2 was cancelled and he was off to sweep leaves in his garden.

It has been revealed that as our sister site GamesRadar+ covered, Sarzyński isn't the only CD Projekt Red game dev impressed. Joint CEO Michał Nowakowski called the game a masterpiece and remarked it's "unbelievably hard" to achieve what Rockstar has. Cyberpunk 2 associate game director Paweł Sasko called it a "generational banger". Witcher 4 director Sebastian Kalemba said he'd love to lose a whole weekend to it, although he's busy hunting monsters for now.

@RockstarGames created a masterpiece that I am planning to explore in the coming weeks and months. Massive congratulations to the whole team who worked on the game. It is unbelievably hard to achieve what you just did. Hats off to all of youNovember 19, 2026.

Over at Naughty Dog, Michael Barclay, who has 19 years in the industry and is working on Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet, mentioned GTA 6 looks to him like "a Bugatti Veyron would to a nervous Victorian child".

Push Square picked up on how Barclay was impressed by the lighting specifically, which he explained is mostly dynamic, yet he notes it looks as good as, if not better than, most baked lighting. That's a big deal in an open world where the weather and time of day never stop changing.

Tim Soret of Odd Tales (The Last Night) joined the thread, saying he can't work out how Rockstar gets so many draw calls, hair simulations and volumetric lights running at once.

I’ve made video games for 19 years and GTA VI appears to me as a Bugatti Veyron would to a nervous Victorian child.November 20, 2026.

None of this surprises anyone who's seen how Rockstar builds its world. As I reported earlier, Rockstar's art team designs buildings by imagining who actually lives in them. And then there's the fact that the animators spend months on small details, like how Lucia opens a door with her hip in a natural way when her hands are full.

VP of art Miriam Bellard notes they ask whether a place is messy or tidy, and "what is their taste?" The range runs from industrial and scruffy to decadent and dangerous.

According to recent reports, so it seems the people who made GTA 6 are as stunned as everyone else by what they've achieved. As GamesRadar+ reported, Rockstar production coordinator Navya Manaswitha reacted to the reviews by saying she's "truly grateful to be a part of this masterpiece".

I've already argued Rockstar has bucked the AI trend in how it made the game, and GTA 6 is proof that human creativity is still the most impressive technology we have. It seems most game devs agree.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This week on Dezeen, we kicked off our 20×20 project, in partnership with Kohler, to celebrate 20 years of Dezeen.

Over the next month, we will reveal the architects and designers who will have the biggest impacts over the next 20 years, as selected by some of the biggest names in architecture and design from the past 20 years.

We started the series with an interview with Harry Nuriev, who was selected by Bjarke Ingels. We then interviewed Lanza Atelier, Freya Tangelder and Swedish Girls, who were selected by Frida Escobedo, Nendo and Sabine Marcelis, respectively.

In a substantial week for Dezeen, we also announced the winners of the 2026 Dezeen Awards winners at a ceremony in London.

We we revealed the architecture, design and interior project winners, including the Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi (pictured), along with the six designers of the year.

In architecture news, recently revealed images of the White House ballroom drew attention to the huge scale of the project, which many remarked “dwarfs” the central residence.

“It states everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People’s House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday,” wrote Hilary Clinton on X.

A group of Harvard GSD students also aimed to draw attention to another Donald Trump-backed scheme in Washington DC, by proposing alternative designs to his planned arch.

The two proposals for the planned site of the arch replaced the proposed structure with an expansive pool of water.

Also in the US, plans by SHoP Architects for a supertall skyscraper in Miami, which is backed by Serbian tennis player Novak Djokovic, were revealed.

The 320-metre-tall skyscraper will have a ribbed design and include amenity facilities developed by the tennis player.

In less serious news, American fast-food chain Chipotle rolled out a range of hoodies all with a hidden, insulated pocket for sneaking burritos into cinemas.

The tongue-in-cheek clothing was designed to keep concealed burritos warm to allow for illicit snacking at the movies.

Popular projects on Dezeen this week include a “surreal” house in rural China, a pink commercial building in Mexico and a Cotswolds barn renovation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Activists against women’s right to choose in relation to their reproductive rights protested a sculpture by Shahzia Sikander in St. Louis this week, calling for the removal of the 18-foot-tall work titled Witness (2023).

Industry observers note that as reported by St. Louis’s First Alert 4, protesters associating the sculpture with pro-choice abortion rights gathered outside the home base of Rung for Women, a nonprofit devoted to women’s career development that hosts it. As the organization describes itself on its website, “Too many women are unfulfilled, unhappy, and underpaid in their jobs, but afraid to take the leap into the unknown. We designed a program to guide motivated women through a process to start working in exciting careers and get paid what they’re worth.” Related Articles Shahzia Sikander's Animated Film Selected for M+ Facade Commission in Hong Kong Shahzia Sikander Indicates She Won't Repair Beheaded Sculpture in Texas: 'A Testament to Hatred'.

Recent findings suggest that first Alert 4 quoted an activist with a group called Students for Life America associating Sikander’s sculpture with the overturning of Roe v. Wade in 2022. “Her skirt spells Hava, which is Eve, the first female rebel, to breathe life,” said Reagan Barklage, who related the work to the late US Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg. “It’s just, you do not need to kill your children in order to breathe life. That’s actually the exact opposite of what that means.”.

She continued: “We’re alarmed that this is what they’re choosing to use to represent our city. We do not stand for these pro-abortion rights. And we’re trying to stand for women and true empowerment.”.

According to recent reports, A counterprotester thought otherwise. “We’re here because this organization that’s located on this block has every right to display whatever artwork they want on their own property,” said Leslie Zacks, who spoke of the protest in the context of a recently failed amendment that would have reinstated a near-total abortion ban. “The reality of the situation is that the people in Missouri have twice had the opportunity to voice their preferences with regards to the abortion problem and have made it very, very clear with increasing majority where their preferences are.”.

Recent findings suggest that rung for Women issued a statement saying the organization “respects the right of individuals to express their views about art, including those that differ from our own. We recognize that Witness has prompted strong reactions and respect the sincerely held beliefs of those who have expressed concern. We remain proud to host this work by Shahzia Sikander at Rung for Women.”.

It has been revealed that the same sculpture by Sikander was the subject of heated protest in Texas in 2024, when it was decried by a group that called it “satanic” before it was to go on view at the University of Houston. After an opening and artist talk related to the work were subsequently canceled, Sikander remarked, “Art should be about discourse and not censorship. Shame on those that silence artists.”.

An attempt by ARTnews to reach the artist was not immediately successful.

Five buildings where the staircase is the facade

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Japanese wedding chapel, an Indian university and a reformed monument to an Albanian dictator are among these public buildings where stairs help to create a dramatic facade.
  • Sources indicate that some, like the MVRDV’s Pyramid of Tirana and Snøhetta’s Shanghai Grand Opera House, were designed specifically to give the public unrivalled access to their architecture.
  • The one thing they all have in common is that they make their stairs the main event.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Japanese wedding chapel, an Indian university and a reformed monument to an Albanian dictator are among these public buildings where stairs help to create a dramatic facade.

Sources indicate that some, like the MVRDV’s Pyramid of Tirana and Snøhetta’s Shanghai Grand Opera House, were designed specifically to give the public unrivalled access to their architecture. Others, like the Ribbon Chapel (top image), use stairs to serve as both a viewpoint and a metaphor.

The one thing they all have in common is that they make their stairs the main event.

Prestige University, India, by Sanjay Puri Architects.

More than 460 stepped platforms are arranged on top of Prestige University in Indore, Madhya Pradesh, which was recently crowned education project of the year at the 2026 Dezeen Awards.

Its 9,000-square-metre walkable roof gradually steps up from the ground to its full height of 28 metres, reducing the visual heft of the building while providing gathering space for all of the university‘s 3,000 students at the same time.

Drawing on the ancient tradition of Indian stepwells, the staircases are organised around courtyards that help to draw sun and ventilation deep into the building, reducing its dependence on artificial light and air conditioning.

Shanghai Grand Opera House, China, by Snøhetta.

Snøhetta has had a thing for walkable roofs ever since its seminal design for the Oslo Opera House in 2008.

Now, China has received its own take on the theme with the Shanghai Opera House, defined by a giant spiral staircase that curves out of the facade and dramatically cantilevers at its peak.

Much like the slanted roof in Oslo, the stairs were designed to make the building radically accessible to the public – although Dezeen revealed earlier this month that access to the roof is now restricted to paid ticket holders.

Pyramid of Tirana, Albania, by MVRDV and IRI Architecture.

Stairs serve both a practical and symbolic function in MVRDV‘s renovation of the Pyramid of Tirana – a monument built for Albanian dictator Enver Hoxha in the 1980s.

The Dutch architecture studio added steps to the pyramid on all sides to allow people to climb and reclaim the building.

“The first time I saw the Pyramid being walked all over by the youth of Tirana, I was deeply touched by its symbolism and by its incredible optimism,” said MVRDV founding partner Winy Maas.

Ribbon Chapel, Japan, by Hiroshi Nakamura.

Intertwining staircases spiral around the glazed core of this wedding chapel in Onomichi, designed by Tokyo-based architect Hiroshi Nakamura.

The stairs, representing the joining of two people in marriage, meet at the top to create a small viewing platform overlooking Japan‘s Seto Inland Sea.

“Just as two lives go through twists and turns before uniting as one, the two spirals seamlessly connect at their 15.4-metre summit to form a single ribbon,” Nakamura explained.

Hisao & Hiroko Taki Plaza, Japan, by Kengo Kuma and Associates.

This student hub was designed by Kengo Kuma and Associates to resemble a natural landform growing out of the Tokyo Institute of Technology campus.

Wooden bleachers and plants help to conceal the building, which is partially sunken into the ground to retain views of the university’s historic clock tower.

The external staircase that descends into the building is also mirrored inside, helping to blur the boundary between interior and exterior landscape.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

L-tyrosine is an amino acid (AKA protein building block) that supports your body, from your muscles to your noggin.

It’s a non-essential amino acid, which means your body can make it on its own, so you don’t have to get it from food.

That being stated, consuming foods high in L-tyrosine or taking supplements could have extra cognitive and physical benefits – here’s what to know.

L-tyrosine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally. Though your bod can prob create enough of the stuff on its own, some research suggests that supplementing with it can boost your mood and help regulate your stress response.

L-tyrosine helps make many vital chemical messengers, such as:.

Supplementing with L-tyrosine is believed by some to boost levels of dopamine, adrenalin, and norepinephrine in particular.

Foods naturally high in tyrosine include:.

Sources indicate that L-tyrosine may improve your memory and mental alertness. Since L-tyrosine increases dopamine availability in your body, experts think it may boost your cognitive performance. In addition to reward centers, dopamine is linked to working memory processes and plays a key role in the brain’s aging process.

In a 2019 review of several studies, researchers found that a higher intake of L-tyrosine was linked to improved cognition. It also improved executive functions like brain flexibility, convergent thinking, and reasoning.

However, researchers noted that L-tyrosine is most effective when dopamine and norepinephrine levels are reduced (which basically means when you feel stressed AF).

Some L-tyrosine supplement companies claim that their products are both mood boosters and antidepressants, but the results are mixed.

L-tyrosine increases dopamine, the feel-good hormone that’s linked to reward processing and also addiction. In general, it’s been shown to be a vital regulator of mood, behavior, and brainpower – so it makes sense that getting enough of it could benefit your mood, too.

Industry observers note that however, the research on supplementation of tyrosine for depression is super dated, so it’s challenging to draw any definitive conclusions RN. (Plus, depression is also a super complex condition that involves more than just dopamine depletion.).

And though there are some people dubbing L-tyrosine “natural Adderall” for its purported beneficial effect on ADHD, so far, there’s no research to support these claims yet, either. (Though it *is* true that there seems to be a link between ADHD and altered dopamine levels.).

Phenylketonuria is a rare genetic disorder in which the body can’t properly process another essential amino acid, phenylalanine.

Since those with the disorder may also be deficient in L-tyrosine, some experts think that supplementing with it could help relieve some symptoms like seizures or skin rashes.

However, according to a 2021 review of several studies, there is not enough evidence to say for sure.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) considers taking L-tyrosine supplements generally safe.

That being stated, it’s not recommended to mix with the following medications:.

It’s not advisable to take it if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding.

Research suggests that L-tyrosine supplementation likely benefits your brainpower under stress. It also may benefit conditions like depression, but more research is needed to know for sure.

Like any supplement, it is a good idea to contact your healthcare provider before adding it to your medicine cabinet, especially if you have preexisting health conditions or take medications.

Tate Liverpool will reopen in fall 2027 after a £30 million transformation with the exhibition “Surrealism: Staging Dream Worlds,” a nod to the museum’s inaugural Surrealist show in 1988.

According to recent reports, the surrealism exhibition will run from fall 2027 to spring 2028 and include works by Salvador Dalí, Eileen Agar and Man Ray. According to Tate Liverpool, the show will also explore the “important role of surrealism in the history of theater and dance” through the movement’s major commissions for stage sets and costumes. Also on view will be Dorothea Tanning’s costume designs for the ballet The Witch, photographs of Sheila Legge performing as the “Surrealist Phantom of Sex Appeal” at the opening of the 1936 International Surrealist Exhibition in London, and material from the archive of Ted Joans. Related Articles Meryl Streep Makes Substantial Donation to National Women's History Museum, Musée d'Orsay Receives Collection of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist Fan Paintings: Morning Links for March 19, 2026 Museum of Liverpool Evacuated by Phony Bomb Threat.

Sources indicate that “Surrealism invites us to see the world differently and what better way to reopen Tate Liverpool. This exhibition will spark imaginations, surprise visitors and reward curiosity, offering a fresh perspective on one of art’s most celebrated movements. It also brings a wonderful echo of the surrealist exhibition that opened our gallery in 1988, while taking visitors on an exciting fresh journey,” said Jemima Pyne, interim director of the Tate Liverpool, in a statement.

Industry observers note that tate Liverpool closed in October 2023 and was scheduled to reopen in 2025, but fundraising difficulties pushed the date back to 2027. The architecture firm 6a architects is redesigning the gallery’s home, an 1846 warehouse on the Royal Albert Dock, as part of a £35 million ($46.5 million) renovation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Hufton+Crow.

UK studio ZHA took visual cues from the riverbank site of this national theatre in Morocco when designing its sweeping exterior form, which encases a trio of performance spaces.

Named Théâtre Royal de Rabat, the performance venue for artists and musicians is located between the cities of Rabat and Salé near to the recently completed Mohammed VI Tower, which is the country’s tallest building.

It is the first project completed by ZHA, formerly Zaha Hadid Architects, in Africa.

Industry observers note that ZHA revealed its proposal for Théâtre Royal de Rabat in 2010. At the time, the studio’s founder, Zaha Hadid, described the design as “secular”.

“It is uplifting to go into a great space, a heavenly space,” Hadid remarked.

“As a performance venue, the Théâtre Royal de Rabat is secular, but it has the capacity to transport the audience to an imaginary space and time.”.

Théâtre Royal de Rabat’s design draws on the topography of its site on the banks of the Bouregreg River, which runs between the two cities.

It contains three performance venues, with its main space being a 1,821-seat theatre, simply named the Auditorium.

This venue is lined with crystal-like, faceted surfaces that the studio modelled on muqarnas – a traditional type of three-dimensional ornamentation found in Islamic architecture.

The walls also double as an acoustic treatment, developed by ZHA with acousticians at Arup “to deliver the highest quality of sound to every seat in the hall”.

The second venue is the Studio Theatre, an adaptable space with retractable seating that ZHA described as “offering a variety of configurations from a flat-floor to a stage with proscenium arch”.

Industry observers note that it has a capacity of 250 people and is primarily intended for experimental performances and rehearsals. However, it can also be transformed into a space for events such as talks and educational workshops.

The final performance space is the Amphitheatre, an open-air venue accommodating 7,000 spectators for large public events.

The Amphitheatre and Studio Theatre have not yet been revealed in photos.

It has been revealed that completing the building is a triple-height foyer, described by ZHA as “canyon-like”. It is animated by interlocking staircases that emulate draped, flowing fabric, culminating at a restaurant with views of the river outside.

“Designed as a space for transition and reflection, the foyer encourages curiosity and dialogue to unfold before and after each performance,” said ZHA.

According to recent reports, théâtre Royal de Rabat uses a mix of air-source heat pumps, ground-source cooling and radiant heating as part of its heating and cooling system, alongside natural ventilation. A rainwater collection system is used for the bathrooms and landscape irrigation.

Elsewhere, ZHA recently completed a performing arts centre in China crowned by a trio of swooping, interconnected volumes informed by traditional Cantonese opera costumes.

Another landmark performance venue that recently featured on Dezeen is the Shanghai Opera House by Snøhetta, which incorporates a giant spiral staircase.

Photography by Hufton+Crow.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Outgoing Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie G. Bunch III reasserted the institution’s independence in a letter to his staff after a leaked document from a Trump aide laid out a sweeping overhaul of its programming and personnel.

“The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote in the letter, which the Upcoming York Times reviewed and first reported. “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programs.” Related Articles Did a Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveal White House Plans to Revamp the Smithsonian? Rep. Jamie Raskin Wants the Smithsonian to Collect and Display Trump's Propaganda, To Teach About Tyranny.

The document, titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Proposal,” was photographed on a laptop that a Trump aide was using on the Washington Metro. As first reported by ProPublica, its 25-item action list includes plans to dismiss top curators and administrators, among them Anthea M. Hartig, director of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, whom the White House has accused of promoting “radical activist ideology.”.

The plan also calls for a new permanent exhibit, “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance,” and another on “Great Families of American History.” It envisions a “Colossus Statue” of George Washington at the museum’s entrance, which would fulfill a request Trump made in September.

The initiative appears to be a work in progress: Photos show the aide brainstorming additions in a notebook. One handwritten entry seems to read “No X-rated exhibition policy,” an apparent callback to a particularly contentious stretch of Hartig’s testimony, when lawmakers questioned her about images of bondage wear in an LGBTQ history exhibition. On Monday, ProPublica identified the staffer as an associate policy adviser with the Domestic Policy Council, the White House office behind a 162-page report that accused the Smithsonian of “extreme political activism that seeks to transform our country.”.

In a recent development, A central complaint of the report was what its authors characterized as anti-white bias at the museum, which they said showed in its promotion of diversity, equity, and inclusion. The report accused one exhibition, “Many Voices, One Nation,” of trying “to convince visitors that illegal aliens are entitled to citizenship, voting rights and ‘belonging’ in America.” (Two weeks after the report’s release, Trump signed an executive order directing that signs be installed outside the museum warning visitors of its “ideological capture.”).

The document glimpsed on the staffer’s laptop laid out latest interpretive guidelines for exhibits, including an explicit end to the Smithsonian’s use of a diversity style guide. The Smithsonian’s strategy for traveling exhibitions would be reviewed, and one show now on tour, “The Bias Inside Us,” would be halted. Grants to “woke third parties,” such as the American Alliance of Museums, would also be reviewed.

The Smithsonian’s online K-12 curriculum would be overhauled to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology.” The “Becoming US” module on immigration, for example, would be deleted and replaced with a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage.”.

According to recent reports, the Smithsonian, a network of 21 museums, is structured to operate independently of the White House. It’s governed by a 17-member Board of Regents: the Chief Justice of the United States, John G. Roberts Jr.; the Vice President, JD Vance; six members of Congress from both parties; and nine private citizens. Legally, the Smithsonian answers to Congress, not the White House, but federal money makes up about 60 percent of its budget. Trump proposed cutting that funding by roughly 12 percent for fiscal year 2026, a threat that ultimately went unrealized.

Sources indicate that bunch, who became secretary in 2019, has repeatedly asserted the institution’s legal independence as pressure from the White House has mounted. The administration has demanded that the Smithsonian turn over internal materials and pushed for the firing of Kim Sajet, the director of the National Portrait Gallery, whom Trump had called “highly partisan.” Sajet ultimately resigned. Bunch has drawn similar attacks: a White House aide reportedly called him a “rabid partisan.”.

In a May interview with the New York Times, Bunch seemed to acknowledge that recent vacancies on the Board of Regents had weakened his position, though he still appeared to have the support of a majority of the board. In September, he confirmed that he would retire at the end of the year.

Recent findings suggest that in his letter to staff on Tuesday, Bunch wrote, “As I have said before, we welcome scrutiny of our work, and even disagreement. The Smithsonian will continue to be driven by scholarship, research and reflection, free from outside influence and in service to the American people.”.

The result: 7,500 miles per segment, consistently, while cash prices climb.

Choosing a laptop for graphic design work isn't the same as choosing one for surfing and emails. And so while the Black Friday sales have discounts on a dizzying array of laptops, not all of these laptops will measure up to your needs.

To make things easier for you, I've picked out the best laptop deals for graphic designers who split their time between home, studio and clients, and need something both portable and powerful.

Some of these deals are in the UK and some in the US, so we've marked each one accordingly. Here's what's on offer, from the cheapest up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Ori Harpaz.

Miami‘s nightlife scene in the 1990s informed the saturated colours and metallic accents used by local studio Evan Edward inside this apartment in the oceanside city, illustrating what the studio calls its “high-impact minimalism” approach.

Designed for an international family with “personal ties to the city’s storied nightlife era”, the Miami Beach pied-à-terre reflects the hedonistic era that left a distinct stylistic impression.

“Aesthetically, there was a rawness to the excess and glamour,” Evan Edward co-principal Josh Evan Goldfarb told Dezeen. It was a particularly exciting time for colour and design in general in the city.

“The city was in its early stages of redevelopment – the original art deco glamour and run-down beach patina were a sublime tropical combination.”.

He and co-principal Michael Edward Moirano set about creating interiors that blend contemporary and vintage furniture and decor to reflect “a more seductive side of Miami”.

In place of a typical South Florida palette of white, beige and turquoise, spaces feature hues of terracotta, burnt orange, burgundy and ochre. These prevalent tones are complemented by flashes of chartreuse, mustard yellow and metallic finishes.

To create a more welcoming space for entertaining, the designers opened the kitchen to the living and dining spaces with the angular island as a central gathering point.

They also connected the foyer to an adjoining unit behind a series of oversized pivot doors.

“The updated floor blueprint completely changed the experience for the clients,” Moirano told Dezeen. “The triangular island is the hub of the space, serving the kitchen and dining banquette area, while also exposing the living area featuring a dramatic view of Biscayne Bay and the Miami skyline.”.

A butter yellow kitchen was paired with richly veined stone countertops that complement the polished-pebble flooring.

The generous island was illuminated by a 1960s five-pendant light feature above, and accompanied by mustard yellow Calligaris bar stools for casual dining and gathering.

Goldfarb was forthcoming about references to personal experiences and spaces.

“One of the references for the kitchen was an artist studio that I visited when growing up in Coconut Grove – the memory is ingrained in my mind’s eye,” remarked Goldfarb. “It was just so airy – up in the trees, open windows, patina on all surfaces and artwork and materials strewn about.”.

“The sense of colour and mashup of materials – stone, tile, painted – it’s hard to forget,” he added.

Nestled into a corner, a banquette with olive-toned Rubelli velvet upholstery wraps a circular stainless steel table, while a pair of 1970s folding chromed-steel and leather chairs provide additional seating.

An adjustable lamp by Tito Agnoli for Oluce with a custom shade extends from the wall to hang over the table.

The mellow tones of the kitchen were contrasted by the fiery orange-red of the pivoting foyer doors – a hue that reappears in a bold artwork above the bed in the otherwise neutral-toned primary bedroom.

Metallic accents are dialled up in the powder room where a silver metal mosaic clads the walls and metallic zellige tiles cover the floor.

Moirano described it as a “very sexy disco-inspired discovery off the foyer”.

“The result is a small but impactful space that captures the project’s more theatrical influences through materiality rather than overt decoration,” the studio noted.

The team describes the project as an example of its “high-impact minimalism, in which architectural restraint provides a framework for distinctive materials, collectible furnishings, and unexpected moments of visual interest.”.

Located on a barrier island along South Florida’s Atlantic Coast, Miami Beach is renowned for its 1920s art deco architecture and more recent influx of luxury hotels.

Another apartment, on the city’s famous Ocean Drive, was renovated by MW Works to include tropical hardwood and sand-coloured plaster.

Inverted nipples mean your chest cherries retract inward instead of protruding outward. They can be a genetic gift or something that happens over time.

It has been revealed that nipple inversion comes in three grades, according to the level of drama. Let’s break it down so you know what’s going on with those inward-facing nips.

In a recent development, grade 1 inverted nipples are like the shy party guests who need a little encouragement to join the fun. They can pop out with stimulation, like a chilly breeze or a gentle touch.

Industry observers note that grade 2 inverted nipples are a bit more stubborn. They can be coaxed out with some effort, but they’re quick to retreat. They might need a bit more attention, mainly if they cause discomfort or problems with breastfeeding.

Grade 3 inverted nipples are the ultimate homebodies. They’re fully retracted and rarely, if ever, make an appearance. These are the most inverted and might need surgical intervention if they’re causing any complications.

Sometimes, you’re born with inverted nipples. Doctors call this congenital inversion.

Several options are available for treating nipple inversion:.

Gentle manipulation and massage with your fingers can temporarily draw out the nipple.

While this method can help with mild cases (Grade 1), it often provides short-lasting results and needs to be repeated regularly.

Useful for chestfeeding peeps! Nipple shields are soft, silicone covers that fit over the nipple and help coax the nipples outward, making nursing easier.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Robert Pattinson is the upcoming James Bond and brings with him a host of luxury deals and an audience that’s grown up alongside him.
  • Recent findings suggest that robert Pattinson has only just got the coveted job as the most famous secret agent on earth, and there’s already speculation around who’ll cut his first dinner jacket.
  • There’s a little bit of danger in Pattinson’s acting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Robert Pattinson is the upcoming James Bond and brings with him a host of luxury deals and an audience that’s grown up alongside him. Matt Kerr, Global Executive Creative Director at Marks, shares what he feels brands will need to do to belong in his version of Bond’s world.

Recent findings suggest that robert Pattinson has only just got the coveted job as the most famous secret agent on earth, and there’s already speculation around who’ll cut his first dinner jacket. Craig wore Tom Ford, but Pattinson has enjoyed a longstanding relationship with Dior. I’m interested in who gets the job, of course – but I’d like to see what Pattinson does in the suit first.

There’s a little bit of danger in Pattinson’s acting. He has this laid-back British cool thing going on, but there’s also a bit of an awkward edge to him – he’s a bit of a conundrum, and I’d s say there’s something of Fleming’s Bond in that. So, for an agency taking a brief or a brand handing one out, I’d start there. What would this particular Bond choose, and when would we get to see why he chose it?

Fleming was deliberate in showcasing what Bond would buy – he understood his protagonist and the pleasure his audience would get from finding out. The Sea Island cotton shirt, the Rolex, the Aston Martin. You could read the books as a shopping list for a certain idea of British masculinity. The list was interesting because it belonged to a man who had his reasons for choosing things.

Take the silver Aston Martin in Goldfinger. An iconic scene is Bond flipping open the top of the gearstick and sending his passenger through the roof. I couldn’t tell you how long the badge was in shot. But the car still got the punchline. Yes, you can hand over some serious investment to get your car brand into a Bond film, but it’s the association with the scene and the interaction with the hero that people buy into.

According to recent reports, I’d give a watch brand the same brief. For No Time to Die, Omega developed the Seamaster Diver 300M 007 Edition with input from Daniel Craig and the filmmakers, then put it on sale to the public. Craig wanted a lightweight watch that felt right for a military man, so Omega made it in titanium. That’s where I’d start with Pattinson too. Work out what his Bond would choose and why. If the audience can see why he’d wear it, they’ve got a reason to want one for themselves.

Brands also need to think about the audience. Yes, Bond is the ultimate masculine icon, but Pattinson is an icon to women in their thirties because they grew up with him. For the teen girl who saw the first Twilight movie at 15, Pattinson is her pin-up. And if he stays with the franchise for the best part of a decade – which seems to be the norm – that young girl will be in her forties. So, I’d have that in mind when I was briefing the campaign.

Take a hotel partnership. There’s a familiar version of that ad where a man books a weekend so he can spend it feeling like Bond. According to Nielsen data, women influence 70 to 80% of consumer spending, so maybe brands should ask what a hotel brand could offer a woman who has followed Pattinson for years and fancies booking the weekend herself. Give her a detail to spot at check-in and let it pay off later that evening. She gets to have some of the fun Bond has in the film. If the partnership carries through to another film, the hotel can give her something different to come back for.

Recent findings suggest that I’d keep the gun barrel iconography and every word of the slick one-liner, “Bond, James Bond”, but I’d give Pattinson room to play with the pause. We know the line so well that we’ll hear the difference. And I’d make this the rule for every brand partner. Make it make sense for Bond but show me what makes it right for Pattinson’s Bond.

When the first design concepts come in, I’d put my thumb over the 007 mark. If the cufflink shot underneath could sell any Saville Row suit, I’d send the team back to the drawing board. It must fit this fresh era of Bond - something that Craig’s or Connery’s might have passed on.

Some of the old partnerships will still fit. Others will need to go or evolve with the way he plays Bond and the audience that will spend the next decade watching him. For a brand planning its next five to ten years, the next Bond film might be the last great monoculture event.

Industry observers note that matt Kerr is a Global Executive Creative Director at Marks with more than 20 years’ experience shaping brands and leading creative teams. His work spans brand identity, packaging, campaigns and digital experiences for clients including LEGO, Diageo, Reckitt and Haleon. At Marks, he has helped transform the agency’s strategic design offering and leads creative standards across a global community of more than 500 designers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Design Museum.

Ten leading designers have unveiled posters that celebrate 10 years of London’s Design Museum in Kensington, which was completed by OMA, Allies and Morrison and John Pawson in 2016.

Originally located in an old 1940s banana warehouse on the south bank of the River Thames, the Design Museum opened at its current site in Kensington, west London, on 24 November 2016.

To mark this 10-year anniversary, the museum asked 10 international designers to create posters for the occasion.

The lineup includes British graphic designer Margaret Calvert, who is known for creating the seminal 1960s Motorway and Transport typefaces with fellow British designer Jock Kinneir.

The hugely popular typefaces were invented to clarify the UK’s road signs and are still used today.

Calvert designed a subtle road sign-style poster for the Design Museum’s anniversary, depicting a fork in the road between Kensington and Shad Thames, where the original museum stood between 1989 and 2016.

Former Apple designer Jony Ive also conceived a poster in collaboration with his studio LoveFrom, which he founded with Australian practitioner Marc Newson in 2019 after his departure from the technology brand.

Ive and LoveFrom‘s poster features a minimalist grey and white design composed of two understated shapes that resemble the number 10.

American filmmaker Tim Burton is also among the lineup and applied his trademark playful drawings to a poster illustrated with two characters sitting atop the number 10.

Burton’s extensive portfolio was on display at the Design Museum in 2024, charting 50 years of his cinematic career.

Dutch industrial designer Hella Jongerius, meanwhile, created a poster depicting a colourful woven tapestry in a nod to her work, which typically blends contemporary technology with traditional crafts.

The other six designers who make up the lineup are London studio A Practice for Everyday Life, Brazilian graphic designer Marina Willer, British fashion designer Paul Smith and British designers Sebastian Conran, Simone Brewster and Tom Dixon.

The Kensington Design Museum is located within the former Commonwealth Institute building.

Dutch architecture practice OMA worked alongside London office Allies and Morrison to restore the shell of the Grade II*-listed building, while British designer Pawson conceived the museum’s interiors.

Images courtesy of Design Museum.
