Skin in the Game: Is Adapalene or Salicylic Acid Better for Acne?

📅 31 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 3 min read (639 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if you have acne, you probably know more about skincare than most people.
  • Sources indicate that but do you know what each treatment does for your skin and if one is better for acne?
  • Salicylic acid is a keratolytic agent commonly found in over-the-counter creams, face washes, masks, and gels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you have acne, you probably know more about skincare than most people. You might even impress friends with terms like “adapalene” and “salicylic acid.”.

Sources indicate that but do you know what each treatment does for your skin and if one is better for acne? Let’s find out!

Salicylic acid is a keratolytic agent commonly found in over-the-counter creams, face washes, masks, and gels. While it’s often used for acne, it can also help with dandruff, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, calluses, and warts.

Adapalene, often known by its brand name Differin, is a topical retinoid. It comes in various forms, such as gels, cleansers, and creams. And just like salicylic acid, it’s available over-the-counter without a prescription.

On a chemical level, adapalene and salicylic acid work in different ways to clear acne.

Salicylic acid breaks down a protein called keratin in the outer layer of the skin. Studies show this helps remove the buildup of dead skin cells. It also reduces inflammation in the skin, calming the redness that often comes with breakouts.

Sources indicate that adapalene, on the other hand, is a retinoid. And what, you may ask, is a retinoid? It’s a derivative of vitamin A that attaches to receptors in the skin. Doing so prompts cell turnover to speed up, helping skin regenerate more quickly and lowering the likelihood of clogged pores.

Industry observers note that so… what do these differences mean for acne? Both adapalene and salicylic acid can treat skin prone to breakouts (though it’s not recommended to use them together since this can over-irritate your skin).

Recent findings suggest that which one is more potent may depend on your acne type. Research shows that adapalene was among the best treatments for comedonal acne (aka whiteheads and blackheads), whereas salicylic acid was less effective and more affordable.

Long story short: Your dermatologist can help determine which is the smarter choice for your type of acne.

It has been revealed that studies haven’t directly compared adapalene and salicylic acid for blackheads, but both can help. Blackheads form from plugged hair follicles, and salicylic acid’s exfoliating action can clear clogged pores. Adapalene increases cell turnover, which can also help remove blackheads.

Adapalene is a retinoid. Retinoids are well-established anti-aging agents because they stimulate upcoming cell growth and promote collagen production. Some studies have also shown anti-aging benefits from salicylic acid.

While salicylic acid, due to its exfoliating properties, can help reduce wrinkles, adapalene is generally more effective for addressing aging-related concerns like wrinkles.

Adapalene is an over-the-counter acne treatment — so prescription-strength options may work better. According to the American Academy of Dermatology, some of the most potent acne treatments include antibiotics and isotretinoin.

Industry observers note that adapalene isn’t a magic wand for acne. It may be an ideal choice for some people, but depending on your skin type and sensitivity level, salicylic acid, other OTC products, or even a prescription treatment might be your best bet.

Research shows that adapalene can be just as strong for zapping zits as benzoyl peroxide (another potentially powerful weapon in the battle against acne). A 2024 study, for example, found that 0.1% topical adapalene was as safe and effective as a 4% benzoyl peroxide solution in people of color.

Sources indicate that though adapalene may be an effective acne treatment, it’s not the pinnacle of retinoid strength. Of the four “generations” of retinoids, adapalene is considered third-generation. Fourth-generation retinoids are typically stronger and have higher specificity to retinoic acid receptors in the skin. For this reason, they’re available only by prescription.

Feel free to experiment with adapalene and salicylic acid to see which works best for you — after all, it’s your face! You might find one more effective for your skin. For expert advice, be sure to consult your dermatologist.

Furniture designers contend with their personal experiences living in New York City through the objects in our most recent roundup.

New York, New York has inspired filmmakers, writers and artists to make work since the city’s inception, and for designers, it’s no different.

The furniture and objects below explore aspects of moving to or living in Newly introduced York City, whether it’s the difficulty of maintaining a career and community, the dissonance of missing home, the architecture, or dead, smooshed rats on the daily commute.

In many cases, the collections reflect on the designer’s own identities and heritages.

These include pieces by Kim Mupungilaï, Rafael Prieto and studio Tian & Teague, all of whom have lived or passed through New York during their practice.

Read on below to see how the metropolis has shaped their work.

What Still Holds, by Bechara Maalouf.

Bechara Maalouf created a series of lamps made out of wooden beams from Lower East Side buildings and intricate screens informed by the window guards at his family home in Lebanon.

The series, first displayed during NYC design week 2026 in May, merged Maalouf’s two homes as the designer grappled with the impacts of Israel’s ground invasion of Lebanon from afar.

Find out more about What Still Holds ›.

Pax Newly introduced Yorkea, by Massimiliano Malagò.

Designer Massimiliano Malagò created an acrylic chair, covered in his own writings, that explores the challenges of maintaining a life in Upcoming York City.

“For me, this was making an object that is incredibly luxurious, incredibly grand, but it’s actually talking about something quite common and sometimes quite sad, because the hardships that people go through to stay in the city are just difficult,” he told Dezeen.

Find out more about Pax Newly introduced Yorkea ›.

Los Angeles and Lisbon studio Tian & Teague created the NYC Series based on their own time living in New York and some of the jarring aspects residents become accustomed to.

The collection, which includes a flattened-rat rug, came about from things seen on the studio founders’ daily commute.

Find out more about NYC Series ›.

White Picket Chair, by Han Seungmin.

Newly introduced York-based designer Han Seungmin created this chair using modular components from the metallic fences found throughout Brooklyn.

First mass-produced in China in the 1980s, the fences are often used in Asian communities around the boroughs, and Han challenged “the idyllic image of the ‘American Dream’ from an immigrant perspective” through the piece.

Find out more about White Picket Chair ›.

HUE/AM/I-HUE/I/AM, by Kim Mupungilaï.

Belgian interior designer Kim Mupungilaï was prompted to design this collection of wood and fibre furniture after a 2018 visit to Latest York that inspired her to explore her half-Belgian, half-Congolese roots.

“I just started thinking about my own cultural landscape and background and upbringing and wanted to dig deeper,” Mupungilaï told Dezeen.

Find out more about HUE/AM/I-HUE/I/AM ›.

The City Block, by Micah Rosenblatt.

Metalworker and designer Micah Rosenblatt looked to Newly introduced York City’s historic architecture for his The City Block collection, which features thin, contemporary lines and geometric elements.

“[The expressions] are based on the cityscape and my relationship to it,” Rosenblatt told Dezeen. “It’s the forms that you would look out and see on your horizon via whatever time period you’re in.”.

Find out more about The City Block ›.

All Other Passports, by Julio Torres and Sabai.

Comedian and actor Julio Torres worked with furniture tech giant Sabai to create his first furniture collection, All Other Passports, debuted during NYC design week 2026.

The collection is influenced by literal and figurative aspects of Torres’ move to New York City from El Salvador, such as a curtain motif pulled from JFK‘s international Terminal 4.

Find out more about All Other Passports ›.

For The Future of the Past, by Rafael Prieto.

Designer Rafael Prieto integrated building fragments into several furniture pieces for an exhibition at Emma Scully Gallery earlier this year.

Prieto sourced the cast-offs, including pieces of a cornice, from a facade being demolished across the street from his Tribeca studio, which he had become “deeply interested” in.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this month, two imaginary worlds collide as the legendary tabletop roleplaying game Dungeons & Dragons joins forces with the wildly popular MMORPG, World of Warcraft.The two fantasy franchises have crossed paths before, albeit obliquely, with Warcraft: The Roleplaying Game in 2003, a standalone RPG that was compatible with D&D's 3rd Edition ruleset. The upcoming D&D: World of Warcraft gameplay expansion book, however, is the first full-blooded crossover to bring the different species, settings and magical items of Warcraft to the beloved D&D 5E ruleset. "It's such an obvious partnership that it was only a matter of time before it finally happened," admits Senior Game Designer James Wyatt, who led the project for D&D publishers' Wizards of the Coast. "Fundamentally, this book is about playing D&D in the world of Azeroth, and giving you the tools you need to do that.".

In a recent development, D&D: World of Warcraft is a lavish 256-page hardback book that takes you back to the magical realm of Azeroth and enables you to explore it in the context of your D&D games. The fresh volume contains 13 WoW-themed character classes for you and your friends to play as, including staples such as Death Knights and Druids, Warlocks and Warriors. It's also chock full of lore that will enable you to devise a rich background for your characters, as well as a wide range of professions and gear that will help them on their adventures. "I like to tell players that they can make a character whose backstory is unique, entirely unlike any other character with the same species," says Wyatt, of the book's flexibility. "You can play a Night Elf with the Sailor background, perhaps having grown up ferrying passengers between Auberdine and Rut'theran, never venturing into the heights of Teldrassil – unlike every Night Elf in the MMO. Or you might choose the Entertainer background for your Orc, deciding that you were part of a small, unloved theater company in Orgrimmar for years before deciding to seek your fortune as an adventurer instead. The possibilities are limitless!".

The upcoming book contains a wealth of new illustrations alongside art that has been carefully selected from World of Warcraft's vast archives. "When I came in, I was like, okay, do we have the resources to do this all from scratch, or are we picking out some of the art [from the archives]?" says Jaramillo. "From there it was about figuring out which artists we would have and what type of visuals we would like to include, because World of Warcraft has several different styles of illustration, right from the beginning, like Chris Metzen's sketches [most of which hail from the early, pre-MMO versions of Warcraft – ed.] and then going through the Alex Horley work to more modern stuff, with Billy Christian and Andrey Kuzinskiy." In total the book contains work by more than 50 artists. In terms of the methods and materials used, the book was a real mix with Jaramillo stating that, while most of the artists worked in PhotoShop and Procreate, some painted with oils and then touched the images up digitally.

It has been revealed that in short, it's a perfect blend of these two iconic games, though adapting an online game into a pen and paper RPG was no simple task. "Different parts of the game presented very different challenges," says Wyatt. "And even each WoW class demanded a different set of solutions as we tried to express that class in D&D terms. The result is a book that I think pushes our design across the board to new levels, and challenges our team to continue to innovate and explore the reaches of what we can do in D&D design."Of course, ImagineFX is first and foremost a digital art magazine and we're excited about the visuals in the book as much as we are the game itself. D&D: World of Warcraft does not disappoint on that level – it's a genuinely lavish affair, with every chapter filled with gorgeous, evocative images that celebrate World of Warcraft's long history. Art Director Sergio Jaramillo led the design of the book in what sounds like a dream gig for the veteran WoW player."I joined the D&D team around two years ago," he explains. "By that time [Wizards of the Coast and WoW-owners Blizzard] were already thinking about getting this project prepped. As I was joining the team, my creative director asked me, 'Is there anything that we're working on that you might be interested in?' and immediately I noted, 'Warcraft!' That is my jam. I was very familiar with the world, so it was a no-brainer for me.".

Recent findings suggest that another consideration that the art team needed to bear in mind was that Dungeons & Dragons books have an established format. "We had to have a visual UX layout," says Jaramillo. "The experience of the book needs to feel like it's a D&D book. With the chapter opener images, if it's a class [chapter] then it needs to feel like that class. The species pages need to inform what different types of characters you might find in a species." So, for example, the image used to illustrate the section on the Orcs is rendered in reds and greens, to reflect the creatures’ different skin tones in the video game. Sometimes, however, a hole would need to be filled with the creation of an all-newly introduced image. "For the professions we found a [picture of] a guide fishing, but we needed at least one Horde image too, so that it didn't look like we're skewed towards just the Alliance," Jaramillo explains. "So we added an image of an undead gathering some shrooms. It was a case of getting the right images that we needed for the game. We had access to all these gorgeous pieces of art and we definitely dug deep into the archives of Blizzard.".

Of course, a massive part of the appeal of both Dungeons & Dragons and Warcraft is losing yourself in a richly-detailed fantasy world. The locations of Azeroth remain a vital part of the WoW experience, arguably more so in this tabletop form where players are relying on the imagination of their DM, rather than graphics, to guide them through an adventure. To help make the dungeons accurate to the game, Wyatt played through the MMORPG's various dungeons, trying to map them out, while Jaramillo worked with cartographers Damien Mammoliti and Marc Moureau. "Their style of art is a little bit different," says Jaramillo. Mark is a bit more comic book-ish, in the work that he does, it's more lines, and Damien is very painterly. So it was like, OK, how do we make these maps and styles look similar and inform [the players] that they belong to World of Warcraft. So we put them on parchment that is very reminiscent of the WoW maps. That's the bridge between these two artists and between D&D and WoW.".

It has been revealed that one of the earliest locations that players will encounter in the book is the dank Blackfathom Deeps, a fallen temple of Elune that has been defiled by the sinister Twilight's Hammer, evil worshippers of the Old Gods. It's Wyatt's favourite dungeon in the book."Blackfathom Deeps holds a special place in my heart for a couple of reasons," he claims. "My first WoW character was a Night Elf, and I spent months steeped in the aesthetic of the Night Elf regions of the world, including Teldrassil, Darkshore, and Ashenvale (where Blackfathom Deeps is located). I love the colors, the landscapes, and the music of those regions, and the hints of the sweeping history of the Night Elves I got as I adventured through those areas. It was also one of the only dungeons that I actually played as part of a group in those early years, where mostly I was exploring the world solo or with my daughter.".

Industry observers note that wyatt hopes that D&D players who have never experienced the MMORPG before will find inspiration for their own campaigns. "Any of the monsters in the bestiary chapter of this book can be dropped into a D&D campaign on any world," he notes. "My hope is that D&D players who pick up this book will realize that Azeroth is a really cool world that has a lot to offer as a setting for D&D campaigns!"And as for those gamers who grew up with WoW and who are coming to D&D for the first time? "I want them to recognize the feeling of being in Azeroth, almost like you were sitting down and hearing the 'Legends of Azeroth' main title for the first time again. And then at the same time to realize with delight that this is an opportunity to explore the world in a whole new way. This is an Azeroth where you can talk to anyone you meet, interact with anything you see, go anywhere you want to, and try anything you can imagine. I can't wait to hear about the stories our players and DMs tell with this material.".

Sources indicate that when it comes to selecting Sergio Jaramillo's favourite image from D&D: World of Warcraft, the Art Director says that he cannot pick just one from the wealth of gorgeous visuals contained in the newly introduced book. "I'll give you three instead," he laughs. "One from the species, one from miscellaneous stuff, and one from the final characters in the book." From the species, Jaramillo chooses an old WoW favourite. "I have to go with the image of the Pandaren. That piece, as soon as it came in, I was like, 'Oh, this just feels right.'"When it comes to the miscellaneous pile, he chooses something more imposing. "I would have to go with the only new class image that we commissioned for the book, the Dracthyr Evoker," he says of a glorious picture of a fearsome and imposing dragon painted by Andrey Kuzinskiy. "That's just great. I really love the energy in that piece."Finally, for the characters, he chooses an image by Alex Horley of a character known in the game as 'the daughter of the sea'. "I think it would have to be the picture of Jaina Proudmoore. Alex just did a really amazing job on that piece.".

Industry observers note that as you might expect, Easter eggs for both games are littered throughout the upcoming book, though both Jaramillo and Wyatt are coy about where you might find them. "The Easter Egg Hunt is less exciting if I tell you where to find them," says the latter, though he points to the piece of art used to illustrate the sections on mounts and companion creatures, noting "The mount and the companion should be recognizable" to fans."I wish I had more time to add even more Easter eggs to this," says Jaramillo. Asked for an example of one that he did manage to sneak in, he highlights a neat nod to D&D. "The art that we picked for the warlock class chapter is of a Gnome. That was just perfect because our warlock art in the D&D book is also a Gnome. So it's like okay, that’s nice. It just fits.".

D&D: World of Warcraft is published by Wizards of the Coast, and is out now.

Sources indicate that will Salmon is Tom’s Guide’s Collections Editor. He has been writing about film, TV, comics, tabletop games and music for almost 20 years, which is quite a long time if you stop and think about it. At Future he rolled out the scary movie magazine Horrorville, relaunched Comic Heroes, and has written for every issue of SFX magazine for well over a decade. His music writing has appeared in The Quietus, MOJO, Electronic Sound, Clash, and loads of other places too.

How YouTube, LEGO, Pokémon, and McDonald's are winning with Gen Alpha

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that what unites the brands that kids love the most?
  • According to recent reports, brands that resonate with Gen Alpha are often seen to be building affinity with the next generation of consumers.
  • Recent findings suggest that but the benefits of engaging Gen A audiences can often be seen sooner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that what unites the brands that kids love the most? Autonomy, discovery, sharing and collecting are recurrent themes, according to Beano Brain's 2026 Coolest Brands report.

According to recent reports, brands that resonate with Gen Alpha are often seen to be building affinity with the next generation of consumers. It's true that many connections formed with brands today will continue throughout adolescence and adulthood.

Recent findings suggest that but the benefits of engaging Gen A audiences can often be seen sooner. Our Gen Alpha: Born to Shop research from earlier this year found that the UK’s 7-to 14-year-olds had £94 million worth of pocket money to spend on the high street.

Autonomy and self-discovery really matter to Gen Alpha, and we see this across some of the most popular brands that ranked in our research.

It’s no surprise when you consider that kids’ lives are still primarily spent following schedules and rules set by adults. Creating a space for them to explore their own interests gives them that freedom and ‘grown-up’ feeling.

In a recent development, youTube – the number one coolest brand for the past three years – is a perfect example of this. The platform lets kids follow creators, explore new hobbies and move naturally between quick clips and long-form content. And importantly YouTube serves up content focussed on kids’ interests that simply isn’t available anywhere else – certainly not in traditional media.

According to recent reports, the same is true of TikTok (#9), which also enters the top ten for the first time this year. But despite the apparent appeal of social media brands, even here kids are increasingly trying to gain control concerned with doomscrolling and other negative online experiences, 49% of 7-14-year-olds having actively taken time off social media; a third of those taking a break wanted more time for hobbies and interests.

Industry observers note that youTube and TikTok are popular with younger audiences because they offer a chance for kids to explore and provide them with a sense of an owned space. But the vital contradiction for brands to understand is that kids don’t want to spend all their time there and that sense of freedom isn’t limited to a screen.

Food, drink, and retail brands consistently score highly in our reports because they lead on innovation for example offering a range of limited-edition flavours and experiences for kids to explore. They’re also inherently shareable and must be experienced offline, - attributes of shareability and real-life experiences are loved by kids.

This is backed up by kids’ preferred shopping habits. In Gen Alpha: Born to Shop, more than two thirds (68%) of kids preferred real shops to shopping online, while 90% preferred shopping with someone.

Retail, and particularly QSRs, offer kids affordable spaces for kids and tweens to spend time with family or friends. This is one reason McDonald's has risen to number two, and why food and drink brands in general account for 29% of our Top 100; they offer the chance for shared real-life experiences kids crave.

The return of toys and physical play also came through strongly.

Analogue toys and collectables tap into kids' love of building, trading, and sharing physical items. LEGO (#6), another top ten brand, not only appeals to kids' creativity, but also, through partnerships, allows kids to collect different sets and get imaginative in a hands-on way.

Sources indicate that pokémon (#34) is another brand that’s ‘cool’ this year. Its cards and merchandise give it a collectible and shareable real-world presence to reinforce the online games and TV highlights, properties that may have been the introduction to Pokémon for kids.

It is these shareable and collectable traits that play into the popularity of food and retail brands. For McDonalds, Happy Meal collaborations give children another reason to anticipate a visit, bringing familiar characters and collectable formats into the experience.

YouTube, LEGO, Pokémon, and McDonald's all share some of the same attributes of discovery, autonomy, shareability, and collectability. In this context, what may seem like ‘surprise’ inclusions in the list – the discount stores Home Bargains (#88) and B&M (#83) – make sense. ‘Coolness’ is not a trend; it’s embedded in your brand's personality and the brand experience.

The lesson is not that every brand needs a viral moment or partnership to be ‘cool’. It is that lasting relevance starts with listening to what children want to do and how they want to feel, rather than where to reach them.

Gen Alpha’s choices may still surprise us. But the motivations behind them should not.

Helenor is an award-winning researcher in the kids and family insights field. With over 30 years of experience in kids media, Helenor is an authority on kids, authoring one of the first white papers establishing key Gen Alpha behaviours.

Industry observers note that helenor designed and manages Beano Brain's unique ethnographic kids panel which means she has her ear to the ground when it comes to all things new and emerging. Her thorough knowledge means she has unrivalled knowledge about what drives kids and their parents, the rhythm of their lives and what they think is cool (or not).

Thai Massage Therapy: Benefits and What to Expect

📅 31 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 3 min read (609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether you unwind with yoga or a relaxing massage, Thai massage combines the best of both worlds, benefiting your mind and body.
  • Thai massage is a special kind of bodywork that blends relaxation with flexibility.
  • Sources indicate that drawing from Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, this ancient technique mixes assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and soothing rocking for 60 to 90 minutes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Feeling stressed? Whether you unwind with yoga or a relaxing massage, Thai massage combines the best of both worlds, benefiting your mind and body. Here’s everything you need to know!

Thai massage is a special kind of bodywork that blends relaxation with flexibility. Think of it as a gentle, full-body, more active experience. It’s all about boosting your flexibility and energizing your body. Just a heads-up: napping during a Thai massage might be a challenge!

Sources indicate that drawing from Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, this ancient technique mixes assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and soothing rocking for 60 to 90 minutes. Unlike Western-style massages at a local spa, Thai massage takes place on a mat on the floor. A certified therapist will work to stretch your muscles and apply pressure along your body’s energy lines, known as sen, to release stress with a graceful, rhythmic touch.

You can schedule a Thai massage at many spas, massage clinics, and even some yoga studios, but make sure you find someone with the proper training and certification to give you an authentic experience.

When you arrive for a Thai massage, you might be given some comfy clothes, like a T-shirt and drawstring pants. You’ll remove your shoes, silence your phone, place your jewelry in a small dish, and settle onto a floor mat. Before the session, let the therapist know if you have any injuries.

If this is your first session, it can be intense, so focus on breathing and relaxing. You’ll likely start on your back, with the therapist beginning on your feet and legs. Since the therapist uses their body weight to guide you, it might initially feel a bit weird. Some discomfort is normal as your body stretches, but don’t hesitate to let your therapist know if anything feels uncomfortable.As the session progresses, you’ll likely switch positions, including flipping onto your belly or trying various other postures. Go with the flow as your therapist guides you through stretches and yoga-like moves designed to open up your joints, move your energy, and release tension. Keep breathing and communicate with your therapist throughout the process.

It has been revealed that as the session wraps up, you’ll enjoy some gentle rocking motions to ease you out of the massage. You might feel sore afterward, especially if it’s your first Thai massage, so hydrate and rest. You’ll likely feel incredibly relaxed, more flexible, and energized.

Preparing for a Thai massage is simple!

Pro tip: Clear your mind and be open to guidance. While the stretches may feel awkward initially, allow yourself to let go. This can help you fully experience the massage’s benefits.

Your Thai massage experience won’t resemble a Western-style deep tissue massage. You won’t be naked under a sheet on a raised massage table, and the massage therapist won’t be using long, deep strokes to work your muscles.The other significant difference is that, like some forms of yoga, Thai massage has a spiritual element based on Buddhism. As they use the weight of their bodies to work on your body, your therapist is also trained to send you kind, loving, healing vibes. The ultimate goal is to help you feel better by allowing your energy to flow throughout your body.

The ancient practice of Thai massage combines assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and rhythmic rocking to unknot your body and get your inner energy flowing. Unlike Western massage techniques, you’ll be fully clothed on a floor mat, with the massage therapist using their entire body to release your tension.

Permit yourself to let go, and expect an active, sometimes intense, full-body experience that leaves you relaxed and energized.

Domes depict constellations of missiles in the night sky at Sharjah Architecture Triennial

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee have created three domed structures that reimagine constellations by mapping military objects in the night sky, which were displayed at this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial.
  • Titled After Night There is Nothing, the trio of installations aim to bring attention to how communities are responding to drones, satellites, rockets and missiles changing the sky above them.
  • Covered in thatch, the three curved wood-and-steel structures are segments of a giant globe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee have created three domed structures that reimagine constellations by mapping military objects in the night sky, which were displayed at this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial.

Titled After Night There is Nothing, the trio of installations aim to bring attention to how communities are responding to drones, satellites, rockets and missiles changing the sky above them.

Covered in thatch, the three curved wood-and-steel structures are segments of a giant globe.

Vinyl lines the inner curves, where Nahleh and Saloojee designed creature-like constellations based on man-made military objects in the sky.

The trio of installations were displayed at three venues at the Sharjah Architecture Triennial – the Al Qasimiyah School, a former slaughterhouse, and in the sandy Al Madam town.

Sources indicate that “This is ‘night sky optimism’ – optimism through catastrophe,” Nahleh told Dezeen. “The night sky we are talking about in this project is not the sky of beautiful stars and constellations, but the contemporary sky filled with drones, satellites, rockets and missiles that are changing the way we understand the sky above us.”.

“The drones, missiles, rockets and satellites eclipse some of the constellations, and sometimes fuse with them,” he continued.

“That fusion is at the heart of this project – how do these technologies, through cultural practices on the ground, begin to morph into upcoming creatures and new constellations that people try to make sense of to interpret the violence of this military technology that is taking place.”.

Nahleh and Saloojee aimed to combine the reality of modern war with mythical storytelling, drawing upon their research into communities exposed to military attacks.

“We have noticed in our research that, especially in geographies witnessing prolonged violence, these objects are producing new mythical creatures – creatures that fuse together technological advancement with epistemic practices and myth-making practices that happen from the ground,” stated Nahleh.

“Most of these creatures, these modern constellations as we’re calling them, are populating the night sky in our drawing alongside pathways of flights of drones, satellites and other things that manifest across the night sky we’ve inherited, rather than the one we lost,” he continued.

“We think of these creatures as ones that attempt to tame the military brightness that is populating the sky around us, be it in the shape of missiles, phosphorus, or flares.”.

As well as depicting creature-like constellations in their inner curves, the structures themselves were designed as creatures – the nocturnal Solifugi spider known to run out the sun and into shade.

It has been revealed that “The project is dedicated to the Solifugi, which is a spider that by nature runs away from the sun, the sun of imperial savagery,” noted Nahleh. “It has a very thick skin to protect it from this brightness, and in its belly is a map of the contemporary sky.”.

According to recent reports, three openings puncture the shell in each of the installations. In the desert site at Al Madam, a vertical cut-out frames a view of the minaret of a distant mosque, and at the slaughterhouse site, a long opening was set at the height of a cow.

Traditional Hakawati storytellers will narrate stories at the installations as part of the triennial, which runs until April.

“The story is difficult, but it’s about finding optimism,” noted Nahleh. “People are carving their own histories on the weapons that are here to annihilate them.”.

It has been revealed that “There’s a paradox here that we have to confront,” he continued. “When libraries are being erased, and people have no more books to publish or things to write on, they’re writing on the weapons that are sent to devour them.”.

“Kids now are finding ways again to dream by placing their wishes upon the shooting stars, which are usually missiles and rockets. It’s a sad and complicated story, but we can no longer escape it by wishing for a sky we no longer have.”.

We rounded up eight highlights from this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which includes a draping shelter that pays homage to the improvised learning spaces created by Virginia’s Black community, and a circular canopy with cut-outs that plot 41 medieval Arabic poetic names for the sun.

Sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026 takes place from 14 November 2026 to 14 April 2027 at various locations across Sharjah, UAE. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

And right now you can buy them in the UK for a record low price of £164 over at Amazon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Swiss watchmaker Mondaine has expanded its Doppio collection with the Solar Skeleton, a timepiece that brings solar technology into the foreground of its design.

Rather than concealing the solar plates beneath the dial, the watch reveals them through a precisely cut circular opening, turning a functional component into a defining visual feature.

The design builds on the distinctive visual language of Mondaine‘s Doppio collection, which is characterised by double-line hands and indexes, a concave dial and a double-domed sapphire crystal.

Mondaine explained that these elements establish a sense of repetition, rhythm and structural clarity, while the exposed solar plates introduce an additional layer of depth and visual interest.

While solar technology is typically hidden from view, Mondaine has taken a different approach with the Doppio Solar Skeleton.

A carefully positioned circular opening around the centre of the dial offers a controlled view of the solar movement, while the outer section retains the indexes to ensure clear readability.

By making the technology visible, Mondaine aimed to bridge the watch’s technical function with its aesthetic identity, without compromising the “clarity and legibility” that define the collection.

Powered by a Swiss Ronda solar movement, the watch converts natural and artificial light into electrical energy, which is stored in a rechargeable battery.

According to Mondaine, a few minutes of sunlight can reactivate a fully discharged movement, while a full charge provides a power reserve of up to eight months in complete darkness.

The brand explained that this technology eliminates the need for regular battery replacements, offering a more resource-conscious approach to timekeeping.

The Doppio Solar Skeleton is available in two versions, each offering a different interpretation of its distinctive design.

The first combines a polished silver 316L stainless steel case with a vegan grape leather strap, bringing together traditional watchmaking materials and a contemporary material alternative.

The second features a polished black stainless steel case paired with a matching mesh bracelet, creating a more monochromatic appearance that emphasises the watch’s clean lines and geometric detailing.

Both versions feature a 41-millimetre case, a discreet date window and a precisely laser-etched Mondaine logo and solar markings.

A double-domed sapphire crystal and water resistance of up to 5 ATM complete the design, “combining refined aesthetics with everyday practicality”.

“With the Doppio Solar Skeleton, we wanted to make solar technology part of the design itself,” said Mondaine.

“By revealing the cells beneath the dial, we have created a watch where functionality becomes a defining aesthetic feature, while staying true to Mondaine’s principles of clarity, precision and Swiss design.”.

The Doppio Solar Skeleton reflects Mondaine’s commitment to iconic Swiss minimalist design, where form and function work together.

By integrating visible solar technology into the collection’s established design language, the watch intends to demonstrate how a functional element can become an integral part of a timepiece’s aesthetic identity.

To find out more about Mondaine and the Doppio Solar Skeleton, visit the brand’s website.

According to recent reports, looking at a cactus with its threatening spikes and tough skin, you might not immediately think, “Yep, that’s a thing I could eat.” But guess what? Some forms of cacti are edible, tasty, and quite good for you!

Check out why it might be a good idea to pal around with nopales, the pads of the prickly pear cactus.

The nopal cactus, also known as the prickly pear or the opuntia, is a shrub-like, flowering cactus native to parts of Mexico, Arizona, the Mediterranean, Australia, and other desert regions. It might be recognized by its multitude of connected pads with flowering blooms. (A pad in bloom looks a little like a flat, green paw.).

In a recent development, nopales flowers are filled with a viscous, seeded substance often used in jams, jellies, pies, cakes, and other sweets. But the stems, leaves, and entire pad (with spines removed, obvs) are also edible. Traditional Mexican preparations include boiling, grilling, and sautéing.

Science is still examining the possible benefits of nopales, so some touted wellness perks are fairly tentative. Here’s a look at what we know about these desert fruits.

It has been revealed that almost any time you see bright colors in edible fruits, it’s a sign they contain antioxidants. This is def true for Nopales!

Older studies have found that the fruit inside their flowers is rich in antioxidants like ascorbic acid, phenolics, and a mixture of betacyanin and betaxanthin. These compounds help fight inflammation by kicking harmful free radicals out of your cells.

According to recent reports, since they combat inflammation, the antioxidants in prickly pear could improve joint mobility. In a 2020 study, people who drank 3 ounces of prickly pear juice daily for 8 weeks had better range of motion and greater ease with daily activities than a control group who drank a placebo.

It has been revealed that research suggests nopales may help steady blood sugar. A 2014 study found that people with type 2 diabetes who ate nopales with a high-carb breakfast had significantly lower blood sugar and insulin levels compared to those who didn’t. However, this study only included 14 participants.

In 2019, a larger systematic review assessed the fruit’s potential for blood sugar regulation. While it found insufficient evidence to support using nopales to reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes, the authors noted it might significantly reduce blood glucose levels.

It has been revealed that showing your liver some love might involve adding nopales (or a glass of nopal juice) to your diet. According to research from 2023, this has to do with prickly pear’s effects on triglycerides. By helping reduce triglyceride accumulation, nopales could relieve stress on the liver.

Whether you’ve overdone it on booze or are down with a stomach bug, it’s important to rehydrate with a drink that contains electrolytes. Consider prickly pear juice as your back-on-the-wagon beverage. It’s got potassium, magnesium, and calcium to help rebalance your electrolyte levels.

If you can track down fresh nopales where you live, cooking it yourself is a fun (if somewhat complicated) way to take advantage of its benefits. If not, look for prickly pear products, such as juices, being sure to check for added sugars.

According to recent reports, you can also take a supplement. Nopales supplements typically contain 500-650 milligrams (mg) per day.

While a prickly pear smoothie or nopales salad can be a healthy addition to your diet, consuming this cactus fruit may have some less-than-desirable side effects, like:.

If you’re upcoming to nopales, take it slow at first to see how your body responds.

Don’t let the “prickly” in prickly pear keep you away from this desert gem. When prepared correctly, nopales are unique, nutritious food. Check ’em out when your fruit basket needs something a little different.

GTA 6 is having a wider impact than just being one of the highest-rated games ever, with a 99 on Metacritic; it’s making other developers rethink what they’re doing. This week, many devs came out and praised GTA 6’s technical achievements, from CD Projekt Red to Naughty Dog, but behind the scenes, those same creators are setting newly introduced benchmarks to complete.

Sources indicate that the impact of GTA 6 is simple: it’s as impressive as all great art is, because it expands what's possible through a captivating vision and flawless execution. And it’s making developers think and rethink.

CD Projekt Red is no slouch when it comes to technically advanced games and graphics, but even they are having that moment. The studio behind The Witcher 3 and Cyberpunk 2077 has admitted that GTA 6 inspires its developers, with joint CEO Michał Nowakowski saying he expects The Witcher 4 to make a similarly huge leap over its predecessor.

As reported on Polygon, speaking during the tech giant's latest investor call, Nowakowski was asked whether the jump from The Witcher 3 to The Witcher 4 would be comparable to the one between GTA 5 and GTA 6. His answer was pretty emphatic.

"Do we believe there's going to be a comparable leap between Witcher 3 and Witcher 4? I think so, yes," he remarked. "I mean, it's been 11 years.".

The studio is working to make The Witcher 4 "significantly better-looking and improved in terms of pretty much every possible facet of the game", adding that players should expect a much bigger jump between the two games.

That's quite a promise, although there's a good reason to be ambitious. The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt is now 11 years old, and while its world still looks fantastic (especially after its recent remaster), the technology and expectations for open-world games have moved on considerably.

It has been revealed that GTA 6 is an obvious comparison, but I'm more interested in what CD Projekt Red does differently. Rockstar has its own way of building a world, and The Witcher's appeal has always been its atmosphere, character design, and strong writing. I don't need Ciri's world to look like Vice City, but I do want the same depth and sense of a living world Rockstar has created. Following this year’s Unreal Engine 5.6 tech demo, I’m sure The Witcher 4 will impress, possibly setting a new standard.

CD Projekt Red is clearly putting a lot of its development resources into The Witcher 4. Its latest figures show 513 developers working on the game, compared with 199 on Cyberpunk 2. The latter is still in the earlier stages of development, so expect that team to grow. The Witcher 4 is currently targeting a 2028 release, while Cyberpunk 2 is further away, and by that time we’ll be in the realms of PlayStation 6 and Unreal Engine 6.

There's also a question of how much money studios need to spend to reach these newly introduced visual standards. Nowakowski was keen to stress that GTA 6 hasn't changed CD Projekt Red's development philosophy, describing its projects as ambition-driven rather than simply budget-driven.

It has been revealed that perhaps that's where the GTA 6 hype is sidelined: few developers have Rockstar’s billion-dollar budgets, and no indie ever will, but CD Projekt Red has UE6 and faith in its artists, technicians, and writers. You still need artists with a clear idea of what they want to create, and developers who know how to bring that vision to life.

Tech Report: "Sacred" archaeological finds become raw materials for design in Ex Situ exhibition

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (991 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New objects made from mammoth bone, leather from the middle ages and stumps from a road built under Roman Emperor Hadrian feature in the Ex Situ project, set to be exhibited soon in The Hague.
  • Initiated and curated by Dutch designer Marisa Klaster, working in concert with archaeologist René Isarin, the project makes use of materials that many in Isarin’s profession and the broader public might consider off-limits for new designs: the finds from archaeological digs.
  • However, while these finds, such as 40,000-year-old mammoth bone and 14th-century ship wood, sound like they belong in a museum, they are in fact deselected – not chosen for inclusion in any archives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New objects made from mammoth bone, leather from the middle ages and stumps from a road built under Roman Emperor Hadrian feature in the Ex Situ project, set to be exhibited soon in The Hague.

Initiated and curated by Dutch designer Marisa Klaster, working in concert with archaeologist René Isarin, the project makes use of materials that many in Isarin’s profession and the broader public might consider off-limits for new designs: the finds from archaeological digs.

However, while these finds, such as 40,000-year-old mammoth bone and 14th-century ship wood, sound like they belong in a museum, they are in fact deselected – not chosen for inclusion in any archives.

Deselected finds are duplicates, common in type, poorly preserved or otherwise judged to have limited future research value.

Recent findings suggest that “The material that you see here is the lowest of the lowest quality,” noted Isarin at a preview of Ex Situ at this year’s Dutch Design Week. “It’s not preserved. It doesn’t belong in a museum. It doesn’t belong in a depot.”.

In fact, if it is not going to be used for educational purposes or reference collections, deselected archaeological finds are required by Dutch law to be carefully destroyed, as they are in many places around the world, said Isarin and Klaster.

Sources indicate that although the materials may be of low value to archaeology, the designers both found this something of a waste. With Ex Situ, they aim to explore a new category of use and preservation for these materials, believing artists and designers have the capacity to tell stories of heritage in a different way to museums.

With the permission of the province of South Holland, they gave deselected materials to nine Dutch practitioners with expertise in crafts such as ceramics, woodwork and glassmaking.

One of the most finished pieces, exhibited in a preview showcase at October’s Dutch Design Week in the Klokgebouw, was by footwear designer and materials researcher Judith Sanders.

Sources indicate that she crafted the foundation posts from a section of the Roman Limes border road, dated to 125AD and built under the emperor Hadrian, into the heel of a pair of high-heeled shoes. Sanders was intrigued by the notion that they could perform structurally once again – this time bearing the load of just one person.

Bold numbers on the sides of the shoe denote where on the dig site the material came from, while a second pair of shoes works leather from the middle ages into a modern-day sneaker silhouette.

Another piece is by designer-maker Daan Simons, who worked with 14th-century wood fragments from a ship that was wrecked and then subsequently used in the construction of Rotterdam.

The texture and existing peg holes in the wood are preserved in his Remembrance Pots, which he imagines holding the ashes of a loved one or a keepsake of theirs, compounding the layers of memory in the vessel.

Klaster and Isarin started on the path to Ex Situ after meeting accidentally at their timber drying kiln, where she was having some wood dried for a furniture project, and he was having the deselected Roman posts dried in the hope they would find another life.

According to recent reports, “Intrigued by their blackness”, Klaster asked Isarin if she could have them, and went on to make a series of tall vases. That was five years ago, and they have been discussing the potential intersection of archaeology and design ever since.

Klaster says that the Ex Situ designers were supported with information about heritage and the finds they were working with, but that the project naturally inspired some trepidation.

It has been revealed that “In the work that they have made so far, you see that they have thought it through, and there is respect in what they made,” stated Klaster. “But the first cut with a scissor or a bandsaw is, of course, a scary thing.”.

It has been revealed that “[One of the designers] was like, can I really saw that in two? And I noted yes, you can. If you have a plan as a designer, yes, it’s yours.”.

That worry will be echoed among some archaeologists, Isarin adds, and he and Klaster’s aim is for the exhibition to promote discussion among the profession.

Industry observers note that “For archaeologists, this material is in a sense sacred,” noted Isarin. “But it’s deselected, so nobody wants it.”.

He mentioned that while reactions have so far been positive, the problem becomes more thorny if the design were to take place in a commercial context – for instance, if Sanders’ shoes were sold by a fashion brand. In that sense, some archaeologists may see this project as opening a Pandora’s box.

“As soon as we enter the commercial world, then I think for many archaeologists it will be, even though it’s deselected material, an interesting debate ethically,” said Isarin.

“Suppose that all this matter, which has no value at all, that somebody gets rich out of it. That would be a disaster for many archaeologists.”.

Nevertheless, Klaster and Isarin think it is a debate worth having.

Pieces in the exhibition come from practitioners ranging from glass artist Bernard Heesen, working with 17th- and 18th-century glass, to conceptual material designer Shahar Livne, working with mammoth bone, and ceramicist Lotte Douwes, working with Roman pottery.

“We have so much rich material beneath our feet, with amazing stories from 40,000 years up to today,” noted Klaster.

The exhibition was previewed at Dutch Design Week, alongside the maximalist installation Everything Moist Seems Alive installation by Maison the Faux and Boris Acket and design collective Show Not Show’s Table of Power exhibition.

According to recent reports, ex Situ: Matter in Translation will be on at See Lab, The Hague, from 5 February to 7 March 2027, with discussion events as part of its programming. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

  • The set for The Fall Off Tour was designed by Los Angeles-based Sturdy to realise J Cole’s ambition to take his hometown, Fayetteville – or “the ville”– “to the world”.
  • It has been revealed that to do this, the studio drew on the historic, two-storey Market House building, which has stood as a local landmark in the city since 1832.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Sturdy.

A nine-metre-tall replica of a town hall in Fayetteville, North Carolina, takes centre stage at American rapper J Cole’s world tour set, which has been created by production manufacturer Sturdy.

The set for The Fall Off Tour was designed by Los Angeles-based Sturdy to realise J Cole’s ambition to take his hometown, Fayetteville – or “the ville”– “to the world”.

It has been revealed that to do this, the studio drew on the historic, two-storey Market House building, which has stood as a local landmark in the city since 1832. Sturdy created a weathered, ivy-covered replica of the structure, which is neoclassical with gothic revival details.

“The Market House was chosen because it’s an iconic piece of architecture historically as well in the town that J Cole’s from,” Martinez told Dezeen.

“I think a massive part of the intention is that he takes home with him wherever he goes; conceptually, the idea was to take ‘the ville’ to the world,” he continued.

“And what better way to do that than something that lives basically at the centre point of the entire city?”.

Other nods to the rapper’s life in Fayetteville include the presence of a Honda Civic car, which Martinez describes as a “supporting actor in the show”.

Positioned in front of the building at centre stage, the car is supported on ties that allow it to be suspended above the stage during specific moments of the performance.

“The car is like a supporting actor in the show that adds a little bit of an authentic take to the performance,” he said.

“His fans know the black Civic, and, at least from my perspective, with this being The Fall Off, the car needs to have a place in the story. It’s part of ‘the ville’,” Martinez added.

The set was designed by Sturdy to be easily dismantled, shipped and rebuilt between demonstrates across the US, Europe, South Africa, Australia and Latest Zealand.

This determined the scale and design of the neoclassical Market House replica, which stretches just over 15 metres and is composed of easy-to-assemble wood and metal components.

The materiality of the structure also allows for J Cole’s performance to extend to the building’s first-floor terrace.

Alongside the structure is a 23-metre-long walkway lined with grass, rocks and a tree stump that doubles as a seat for the artist.

“Any show that we are doing, especially of this scale, has to be designed from a ‘rigging perspective’ to how this thing breaks down,” Martinez explained.

According to recent reports, “That all has to be thoroughly thought out because we’ve got to be able to have the proper Legos. We can’t really just show up and hope that it’s going to piece together,” he added.

Also contributing to the set is a large LED screen, which, according to Martinez, is used “rather sparingly” throughout the performances to bring the stage design to the fore.

“I think for a long stretch of time shows were just about crazy visuals and putting stuff on screens and just letting people see stuff moving in the background,” he said.

Sources indicate that “We never use the entirety of the screen for the whole show,” Martinez continued. “It’s to add a little bit of depth to what we have going on scenically on stage.”.

In a recent development, J Cole’s The Fall-Off World Tour has been running since July, with recent shows at London’s O2 Arena. The tour will end in December in Johannesburg, South Africa.

Other set designs recently featured on Dezeen include Dave’s London show, which Stufish illuminated with a laser-shooting piano.

#125896. This optical illusion has stumped scientists for decades, and things just got weirder

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (592 w)

This optical illusion has stumped scientists for decades, and things just got weirder

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We love a good optical illusion, and we've seen plenty of mind-benders over the years, but there's one really famous one that continues to intrigue scientists.
  • A lot of people see it that way, but some people don't.
  • This optical illusion was named after Franz Carl Müller-Lyer, its creator.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We love a good optical illusion, and we've seen plenty of mind-benders over the years, but there's one really famous one that continues to intrigue scientists. The Müller-Lyer illusion looks so simple: two lines, one with arrows pointing inwards from the ends and one with arrows pointing out. One looks longer than the other, right?

A lot of people see it that way, but some people don't. Some people can immediately tell that the two horizontal lines are actually the same length (see below if you don't believe me). But the reason for this difference in perfection continues to be a topic of big debate.

This optical illusion was named after Franz Carl Müller-Lyer, its creator. Many people initially assume that the line with the arrows pointing inwards is longer than the other. But then research published in the 1960s claimed that people in African and Southeast Asian countries weren't so often fooled by the illusion. It seemed that WEIRD people were mode susceptible – that is, people whose backgrounds were Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich and from a Democracy.

That led to a theory that the apparent difference might have something to do with people in industrialised societies being more exposed to sharp angles and straight lines when growing up, and that this somehow moulds their perception.

Industry observers note that the problem is that the suggested difference in perception has now been called into question. As reported by Sciencing, Dorsa Amir and Chaz Firestone, anthropologists at Duke and John Hopkins, have gathered evidence opposing the theory developed in the 1960s and published their findings in the Psychological Review.

Industry observers note that they note that many variation of the Müller-Lyer illusion have been developed, including ones that work in a similar way despite using curved lines instead of straight ones. Other similar illusions abound, including the Ebbinghaus illusion, in which two identical dots are perceived to be different sizes depending on whether they're surrounded by six large dots or eight small dots. In that case, there are no lines or angles at all.

In a recent development, amir and Firestone also turned up flaws in the case studies from the 1960s, and found that later reports had misconstrued the original findings. The evidence that Africans and Asians aren't fooled by the Müller-Lyer illusion appeared to be very scant.

In a recent development, but one discovery would seem to be even more conclusive in disproving the old WEIRD theory. The optical illusion has been tested on people who were born blind and later had lens replacement surgery, and it appears to trick people immediately after they gain sight despite them not having grown up seeing lines and angles around them.

With the WEIRD theory ruled out, it seems then that this old optical illusion has become weirder, becoming a mystery again.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smiling for selfies should be fun, not painful! If cracked lip corners or angular cheilitis make it hard to smile, eat, or kiss, don’t worry. Check out these tips to heal those cracks rapidly. With some care and good habits, you’ll have pain-free, makeout-ready lips in no time. Say goodbye to angular cheilitis and hello to a happier smile!

It has been revealed that the first step to healing your cracked lip corners rapidly is to lock in any moisture. Reach for a product dermatologists call an occlusive, which creates a protective barrier that prevents your lip corners from getting drier. Vaseline, Aquafor, or CeraVe ointment are common occlusives that will help reduce cracking.

Recent findings suggest that dab a little coconut oil, olive oil, or fragrance-free moisturizer on the corners of your lips daily after you shower. Make it a daily habit, but don’t go overboard. A little dab will do. Allow your skin’s natural oils to build back up as the cracking fades. Bonus tip: Add the occlusive lip barrier after moisturizing.

Locking in moisture only works if you have enough moisture, so staying hydrated is key! Keep a refillable water bottle with you as your trusty sidekick. Sip on plain water throughout the day, or jazz it up with a splash of cucumber or another non-acidic flavor. Pro tip: Avoid lemon juice, which can irritate and sting sensitive skin.

Bonus: Staying hydrated will help your raw lip corners heal quicker and improve your skin’s overall health.

Have you noticed that moisture is a common theme here? Lend your lips a humid hand by sleeping with a humidifier beside your bed. Adding moisture to the air is especially helpful for your cracked lips during the winter or in hot, dry climates. Think about popping a small humidifier in your workspace or wherever you spend the most time.

It might seem like a quick fix to lick your lips to keep them moist, but that can make things worse. Saliva evaporates rapidly, leaving a sticky residue that can attract bacteria and lead to infection. So, keep your tongue away from your lips and remember this: “Licking your lips will cause them to lickety-split.”.

Sources indicate that whether from frigid cold or dry heat, your skin can lose water rapidly, causing cracking, flaking, discoloration, or swelling. So avoid jumping from a sweltering afternoon at the beach into a freezing cold movie theater.

Recent findings suggest that also, skip the hot showers or cold plunges for a bit. These types of rapid temperature changes will promptly dry out your lip corners. Bonus tip: Your lips can take a beating from the sun, so find a lip balm with SPF protection.

Industry observers note that if your cracked lip corners don’t improve or become especially painful or swollen in a few days, it’s time to visit a board-certified dermatologist. If left untreated, angular cheilitis can last for years, leaving your lips discolored or scarred.

FYI: Angular cheilitis might not appear as clearly in people with darker skin. Instead of turning red, the affected skin may look pale and have a darker border.

Remember that lickety-split mantra? It’s for real. Saliva can get deposited in the corners of your lips for many reasons, like drooling, smoking, or sleeping with your mouth open due to some sniffles. Bacteria grows in those little saliva pools, triggering an inflammatory response that causes your lip corners to get irritated and crack.

Sources indicate that following these tips will make your lips feel better in about a week. Really bad cases of angular cheilitis can take a few weeks. Avoid smoking and eat a balanced diet to get faster results.

As mentioned above, Vaseline and other occlusives help create a protective barrier over the cracked lip corners, which helps the healing process.

You might have woken up with cracked lip corners, but you won’t be able to get rid of them overnight. Be patient and follow the tips above!

RIBA president rejoins ARB register to restore architect title

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (577 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The president of the Royal Institute of British Architects, Chris Williamson, has decided to renew his membership with the Architects Registration Board, nearly a year after terminating it.
  • In a LinkedIn post, Williamson said he was rejoining the Architects Registration Board’s (ARB) register because he no longer wanted “to face the prospect of legal action”.
  • Specifically, he said he feared the potential “legal proceedings and financial penalties” from referring to himself as an architect, which ARB does not permit if a person is unregistered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The president of the Royal Institute of British Architects, Chris Williamson, has decided to renew his membership with the Architects Registration Board, nearly a year after terminating it.

In a LinkedIn post, Williamson said he was rejoining the Architects Registration Board’s (ARB) register because he no longer wanted “to face the prospect of legal action”.

Specifically, he said he feared the potential “legal proceedings and financial penalties” from referring to himself as an architect, which ARB does not permit if a person is unregistered.

Williamson’s post comes nearly a year after he revealed he was not going to renew his membership to draw attention to what he called the “absurdity of the current regulatory framework”.

This ARB framework currently only regulates the protected title “architect” and the competence of those on its register, meaning it does not oversee the competence of unregistered providers of architectural services.

His withdrawal from ARB last year aligned with the launch of a campaign by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) calling for a upcoming regulatory model for UK architects.

Though he has now rejoined the ARB register, Williamson mentioned his position on the need to reform remains unchanged.

“Today, I have decided to rejoin the ARB register,” he posted on LinkedIn on Friday.

“Over the last year, I have sat in meetings and roundtables with Ministers, MPs and Peers, spoken at party conferences and COP31, and had the pleasure of awarding the Stirling Prize,” he continued. “Throughout, I have felt the fear of legal proceedings and financial penalties all for referring to myself, in these settings, as an architect – something that’s so fundamental to my identity.”.

Williamson, the co-founder of Weston Williamson + Partners, began his two-year term as president on 1 September 2025.

In the LinkedIn post – a shortened version of an open letter shared with RIBA members – he noted he will now continue to “push for a stronger system” for regulation.

The current RIBA campaign calls for three steps to reform architects’ regulation, including repealing the Architects Act – a UK law that sets the framework for the regulation of the title architect, under which ARB is the regulator.

It also proposes newly introduced legislation outlining reserved activities, such as submitting full planning applications, and who can execute them. The final step calls for the introduction of a Built Environment Council to oversee the competence of individuals and companies working in the construction industry.

“I know my decision to return may surprise or disappoint some of you, particularly those who followed my lead,” concluded Williamson.

“I want to stress this is not a step backwards and it does not reflect a change in my views. In fact, the year I’ve spent outside of the Register has only cemented my commitment to reform,” he continued.

“While my title may change, RIBA’s campaign for regulatory reform will not. I will use my experience on both sides to push for a stronger system that protects what we call ourselves – and what we do.”.

In a recent development, williamson was selected as RIBA president in 2024. Prior to this, he held several roles within the RIBA, including the vice president international from 2017 to 2019.

In 2014, ARB gave Dezeen 14 days to amend an article describing John Pawson as an architect, claiming it was “in the public interest” for Dezeen to use an alternative description, as Pawson is not registered with the board.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.
  • According to recent reports, most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down.
  • Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.

According to recent reports, most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down. But if the green becomes a recurring (fecal) matter, it might be something else.

Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.

Spotting green or another unexpected color in the toilet can be startling, but it’s more common than you might think. From dietary influences to your body’s digestion speed, several factors can change poop from earthy tones to other shades. Let’s check some out.

Industry observers note that are you chowing down on lots of green leafy veggies like spinach, kale, or broccoli? These foods are high in chlorophyll, which can dye your doodles green. Chlorophyll doesn’t always break down entirely before reaching your intestines, meaning it passes through your system and colors your stool green.

In a recent development, have you ever had a St. Paddy’s Day-themed milkshake or a brightly colored cake? Artificial colors in foods and drinks can change poop from brown to green. It’s not magic! It’s just the dye in green food passing through your gut unchanged.

When your digestive system processes food too rapidly, it doesn’t allow for the full breakdown of bile, a yellow-green fluid that aids digestion. This often results in a greenish stool, especially during fast-moving episodes of diarrhea.

Have you recently been taking antibiotics? These meds can reset your gut’s bacterial crew. Since these tiny critters play a major part in the shade of your stool, introducing antibiotics might cause green poop sometimes.

If you’ve had certain medical treatments, it can affect digestion and cause bright green poop. One example is graft-versus-host disease, which may occur with bone marrow transplants. This tricky condition can bring about less-than-welcome guests, like diarrhea and green stool. It’s a clear signal from your body that things are out of sync.

In a recent development, some uninvited microscopic guests like Salmonella bacteria, the water-loving mini parasite Giardia, and norovirus can also be a reason for your poop turning green. These critters can hustle your digestion at an unnaturally quick pace, turning your stool green as they disrupt your gut’s usual rhythm.

Babies can surprise you with a whole crayon box of poop colors, and green is definitely in the mix.

For infants, green stool might stem from the same factors as adults, like dietary changes. This includes adjustments when they start eating solids or changes in a parent’s diet if chestfeeding.

Another harmless cause could be ingesting a small amount of amniotic fluid in the womb. So, if you notice your little one sporting some spring grass-colored diapers, it’s usually no biggie.

It has been revealed that if the green theme park in your toilet isn’t closing down, or if it’s accompanied by other symptoms like severe stomach pain, nausea, or diarrhea, it might be time to call in the pros. Persistent changes in stool color may signal underlying health issues that need medical attention.

Dark green poop can result from eating lots of leafy greens or foods with green coloring. However, it can also indicate that food travels quickly through the digestive system.

Industry observers note that while liver concerns can change stool color, they usually turn it pale or dark, not green. If you’re worried about liver health, look for pale or clay-colored stools instead.

If you haven’t been on a kale-eating spree, dark green poop might be from iron supplements or constipation remedies, which can also give poop a greenish tint.

Dark poop could be a sign of your diet or medications. However, if it’s black and tar-like, it might mean bleeding in your upper gastrointestinal tract. In that case, chatting with a healthcare professional is a must.

In a recent development, while green poop can def throw you through a loop, it’s usually not a sign of anything serious. It’s often your body’s way of dealing with what you eat or how fast you digest. So, unless it’s paired with other worrying symptoms, there’s probably no need to panic.

Alien Breed 35th Anniversary Collection review: A brilliant slice of gaming history
