#125850. 5 Signs You’re in a One-Sided Friendship, According to Experts

📅 19 Jul 2024 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1035 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

5 Signs You’re in a One-Sided Friendship, According to Experts

📅 19 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1035 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship.
  • Sources indicate that most friendships will never be truly 50/50, but at the very least they run on an unspoken agreement: both people show up, reach out, and add some fuel to the tank that keeps the engine going.
  • You might notice in small but telling ways: Looking back at your messages, it dawns on you that you’re initiating every conversation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship. Because truth is, our platonic relationships are often the most complicated. Send us your friendship dilemmas here, and we might feature one in a future column.

Sources indicate that most friendships will never be truly 50/50, but at the very least they run on an unspoken agreement: both people show up, reach out, and add some fuel to the tank that keeps the engine going. If that balance consistently feels off—not just once or twice, but over the course of weeks or months—it’s hard not to wonder whether something deeper is going on.

You might notice in small but telling ways: Looking back at your messages, it dawns on you that you’re initiating every conversation. They call, if at all, only when they’re bored or when it’s convenient. And then there’s the sharper sting of noticing how effortlessly they find time for other people—just not for you (a surprisingly common frustration you can read more about here).

To be fair, life can get in the way—people get busy, schedules clash, and our friends can’t always be as available as we’d like—but that doesn’t make it any less frustrating or stop you from feeling resentful when you’re waiting days for a simple “How are you?” But how do you know if this is a temporary lapse or a more unhealthy one-sided friendship? Here are the biggest red flags therapists want you to watch out for.

Look through your texts and DMs: Are you always the first to send a message? When’s the last time they suggested hanging out? You can also experiment by not reaching out to see how long it takes for them to initiate contact. If weeks (or months) go by without a word, their silence may indicate who’s really holding this connection together.

“At a minimum, a good friend (even a busy one) will periodically check in out of curiosity and interest,” Tiana Leeds, LMFT, a therapist based in Santa Barbara, California, tells SELF. After all, someone who truly cares about you should want to know what’s going on in your life, which is why if they consistently don’t try to get in touch (or only expect you to do so), they may not be genuinely interested in your world.

Venting to your friends is natural—some would even argue it can strengthen your bond. That stated, being there for each other is supposed to be a two-way street, Hope Kelaher, LCSW, author of Here to Make Friends: How to Make Friends as an Adult, tells SELF.

According to recent reports, if someone unloads their laundry list of problems but doesn’t listen to yours, “they’re likely using you as their on-call therapist,” Kelaher says. This one-directional dynamic could look like a person who constantly complains about their boss but changes the subject whenever you open up about your work-related stress. Or they dominate dinner conversations with their dating disasters, yet they’re “busy,” uninterested, or MIA when you need relationship advice. Over time, investing all your time and energy into people who won’t give back can drain your energy, Leeds says, and leave you feeling neglected by a person who’s supposed to have your back.

Maybe they insist on eating at restaurants near their place, which means you have to travel across town every single time. They only reach out when “better” plans fall through (“Hey, my dinner got canceled. What are you doing tonight?”), making you feel more like an afterthought than a priority. More subtly, perhaps they’re only interested in brief 15-minute coffee chats that fit their schedule instead of a dedicated dinner or movie night.

“In a healthy relationship there should always be a give-and-take,” Kelaher states, meaning both people need to compromise. So it’s disheartening when, again and again, someone you’d do anything for won’t meet you halfway (sometimes literally).

Recent findings suggest that your friend might be a workaholic or chronically forgetful (which, don’t get us wrong, is still frustrating). But that alone doesn’t mean your bond is one-sided.

Instead, “consider the bigger picture and ask yourself, ‘Is their behavior a reflection of not caring about me, or just a difference in availability and communication style?’” Leeds claims. As an example, someone who takes five business days to reply to anyone’s messages may not be singling you out. What’s more telling, though, is if that same person who’s “too swamped” to text you regularly posts Instagram stories of brunches, dinners, and post-work meetups with others in their social circle. Or if your usually punctual friend (who’s known for being reliable) is comfortable canceling plans only with you. These inconsistencies, Kelaher says, suggest that they’re perfectly capable of showing up—just not for you.

Let’s say you mentioned how key it would be to have support at your first 5K race. A friend who truly cares might surprise you at the finish line with flowers, or at the very least shoot over a heartfelt “Good luck!” or “Congrats!” In a one-sided friendship, however, this kind of consideration may be missing entirely. They might downplay your achievement (“Sorry I couldn’t make it, but it was such a short race!”) or forget your massive day without a hint of apology.

Sources indicate that true friends go the extra mile to celebrate your successes and be there during tough moments. That’s why if someone repeatedly forgets significant events like your birthday, or rarely shows empathy for your challenges (like a scary medical procedure, a high-stakes presentation), they may not be as invested as they should be.

Therapists recommended bringing up your concerns non-confrontationally.

It has been revealed that ideally, their response can give you a glimpse into whether they’re aware of this imbalance and, more importantly, if they’re willing to work on it. That said, you can’t force someone to be a good friend, so if they don’t care enough to show up for you, know that you deserve better. “After all, friendships take work, Leeds says. “But it’s not meant to be done by just one person.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Located outside of Chicago on a lakeside hill, the Women’s Leadership Center contains meeting spaces for established and emerging women in leadership roles to gather and “ideate solutions to complex concerns within their industries”.
  • In a recent development, “Women leaders spend much of their careers in rooms that weren’t designed with them in mind,” mentioned the center’s founder Ann Drake, former CEO of supply chain provider DSC Logistics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy Studio Gang.

Architecture practice Studio Gang has completed a women’s conference centre overlooking Geneva Lake in Wisconsin, with three irregularly shaped buildings informed by the site’s oak forest.

Located outside of Chicago on a lakeside hill, the Women’s Leadership Center contains meeting spaces for established and emerging women in leadership roles to gather and “ideate solutions to complex concerns within their industries”.

In a recent development, “Women leaders spend much of their careers in rooms that weren’t designed with them in mind,” mentioned the center’s founder Ann Drake, former CEO of supply chain provider DSC Logistics. “I wanted to build one that was.”.

Studio Gang said key elements of the design were sustainability – with strategies such as a mass timber structure – and responding to the ecology of the site through gently curving volumes and wide-open windows.

“We designed the Women’s Leadership Center to respect and learn from its surrounding forest ecology while allowing community, leadership, and collaborative problem-solving to thrive,” said Studio Gang founding partner Jeanne Gang.

“Locally sourced materials, mass timber, and low-carbon concrete minimise the buildings’ carbon footprint, while the landscape helps to repair the site’s ecology and enhance its biodiversity.”.

The campus contains three main buildings — the circular Council building that functions as the main meeting space, the Lodge, which is made of three interconnected volumes, and the Cabin, a smaller building that contains accommodations.

White oak wood harvested on-site, a dark wood cladding and natural Wisconsin stone were used throughout all three buildings to “reflect the tones and textures of the forest”, according to the studio.

The Council building is arranged around a central courtyard and garden that doubles as a rainwater-collection site.

Its rooms, including a larger lecture hall and meeting room, fan outwards around the courtyard and are lined with floor-to-ceiling windows, while a heavy timber structure creates a series of skylights at the entrance.

A walkway leads out the back of the Council building towards the Lodge. The building contains more casual meeting and socialising spaces, such as a Great Room arranged around a fireplace.

It also contains a mass-timber structure above this space, which is lined with skylights. Outdoor terraces overlook Geneva Lake, while the building’s green roof contains a “coffee nook” and patios for seating.

Tucked off into a corner of the site, the Cabin building contains several bedrooms across two levels, as well as utility spaces such as a laundry room.

Its lower level contains a dining area and living area, which double as additional, more intimate gathering spaces.

Fully accessible ramps interconnect all three structures and lead down to the water bank, where they end in a pier.

Elsewhere, Studio Gang recently completed an open-air theatre in upstate Fresh York and a Denver hotel.

Photography courtesy Studio Gang.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Magnesium is found in fatty fish, leafy greens, whole grains — and the supplement aisle.

The mighty mineral plays many essential roles in our bodies, but can it help tighten the belt buckle?

We checked in with a doctor to find out.

While magnesium can sneakily support weight loss in a few ways, that’s not its main gig.

“Magnesium alone is not a magic bullet for weight loss,” indicates Paunel Vukasinov, MD, a dual board-certified internist and obesity medicine specialist with Medical Offices of Manhattan.

“A comprehensive approach including diet, exercise, and other lifestyle changes are essential,” Vukasinov adds.

Here are a few ways magnesium may support weight loss, as explained by Vukasinov.

“Magnesium is not classified as an appetite suppressant,” Vukasinov notes.

Recent findings suggest that “However, by potentially stabilizing blood sugar and insulin levels, magnesium may reduce cravings and help prevent overeating. This effect can indirectly support weight loss.”.

Vukasinov reminds us that no specific magnesium dosage is prescribed solely for fat loss.

With that in mind, the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for magnesium is:.

Vukasinov notes that sticking to the RDA ensures you meet your body’s needs without over-supplementing.

“Excessive intake does not enhance weight loss and may lead to adverse effects,” he adds.

According to Vukasinov, it’s best to get magnesium from food since a nutrient-dense diet, including whole foods, boosts your intake of other extra essentials like fiber, which improves overall health.

Here are some foods you can gobble up for the most magnesium:.

If you know your diet isn’t cutting it, you can find magnesium supplements at major retailers, like Wal-Mart and Target, drug stores, or Amazon.

PSA: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not check the safety or effectiveness of dietary supplements, so it’s notable to choose a reputable brand that undertakes third-party testing to prove the purity and quality of their products.

For some, magnesium supplements may cause a few unsavory side effects, including diarrhea, stomach upset, or cramping.

Remember that there are many forms of magnesium. Vukasinov points out that magnesium citrate or magnesium oxide can have a laxative effect (yikes).

Be sure you’re taking the best dose based on your RDA, and consider taking it with a meal to better avoid side effects.

Magnesium is not a miracle solution for weight loss, but getting enough of it can ensure that your body produces enough energy and gets enough sleep — both play a massive hand in weight management.

Taking too much will have you gripping your belly with stomach pain or diarrhea, so stick to the daily recommended amounts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A contemporary take on Ukrainian vernacular buildings and a preschool in Estonia are among the winners of the Thermory Design Awards 2026, which celebrate the versatility of thermally modified wood.

Of 78 submissions from 23 countries, four winning projects have been selected in the competition’s fifth annual edition, covering the categories of interior, tiny and private house, residential, commercial and public building, and wellness and spa.

Thermory thermowood is wood that has been modified using heat and steam with no added chemicals.

The treatment enhances the material’s dimensional stability and reduces moisture uptake compared with untreated wood, according to Thermory.

The winner of the interior category is a trio of Ukrainian guesthouses collectively named Under the Reed Roof, designed by Kyiv-based studio YOD Group.

Each guesthouse comprises a glass-walled volume at the base, topped by a tapered thatched roof with exaggerated proportions.

While the exterior of these roofs is made with traditional reeds, the interiors are lined with thermo-ash shingles, arranged to create a tactile effect that is repeated on the front doors.

These highlight the interplay between the interior’s traditional and contemporary design elements, contrasting materials, and the balance between the structure’s openness and enclosure.

“The project stood out to the jury for its exceptionally coherent concept, in which architecture and interior elements come together to form a harmonious whole,” said Thermory.

Winning in the tiny and private house category was Marker Architecture‘s Flooded Gums project, a flood-resilient dwelling built on working farmland.

The building features thermo-ash cladding and thermo-spruce decking, owing to the materials’ robustness and aesthetic merits.

“What particularly impressed the jury was the honesty and clarity of the architecture,” said Thermory of the project.

“Rather than concealing its construction, the project makes its structural logic visible, with every element serving a purpose: the result is a modest yet highly refined building that strikes a compelling balance between aesthetics, functionality and its natural setting,” it added.

Estonia’s Rakke Kindergarten secured the win in the residential, commercial and public building category, thanks to what Thermory describes as local studio Arhitekt Must‘s “cohesive and imaginative design”.

Thermo-spruce cladding, thermo-pine posts and thermo-pine decking all feature in the design, enhancing both its functionality and visual appeal.

The building’s function as an educational environment is made distinctive by the space’s inventive ceiling, which is composed of the short thermo-pine posts, arranged in a way that creates an engaging optical illusion.

“This unexpected architectural gesture elevates a functional space into something distinctive, demonstrating how thoughtful detailing can shape the character and experience of an entire building,” said Thermory.

Finally, the winner of the wellness and spa category is a sauna within the Estonian Embassy in Berlin, designed by interior studio AERIS.

The interiors feature statement walls covered in custom-made oak shingles, which, being circular and slightly overlapping, resemble fish scales.

These are joined by thermo-alder benches and walls, creating a cohesive scheme of timber details that integrate neatly with the lighting design.

“The harmonious interplay of materials, surfaces and light imbues the space with a contemporary edge while retaining the intimacy and warmth of a traditional sauna,” remarked Thermory.

“Although vastly different in character and purpose, the winning projects share a creative and unconventional approach to design,” it added.

“Each places wood at the heart of its architectural expression, combining imaginative thinking with meticulous attention to detail.”.

The 2026 instalment of the competition was judged by a diverse international jury of architects and Thermory representatives, including Kärt Kanarbik, Thermory’s architectural project manager; Lars Skjølstrup Østergaard, lead design architect at Henning Larsen; Sami Rintala, professor and architect at Rintala Eggertsson Architects; Jaan Port, architect and partner at PIN Arhitektid; and Tõnis Kalve, architect at ByKalve and Thermory project sales architect.

To learn more about Thermory, visit its website.

Yes, Your Feet Age. Dermal Fillers Can Help

📅 13 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A long training walk ahead of the Camano de Santiago.
  • Recent findings suggest that using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not latest, though it is gaining in popularity.
  • Over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Barefoot walks on the beach. A day in their favorite high heels. A long training walk ahead of the Camano de Santiago. These are the goals—big and small—of women undergoing foot filler treatments.

Recent findings suggest that using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not latest, though it is gaining in popularity. As early as the 1960s, medical-grade silicone has been used to puff up padding deflated by age, years of wear and tear, and fashionable footwear, especially high heels. All of this puts intense pressure on the balls of the feet—otherwise known as the metatarsals.

Over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates. Fat pad atrophy affects 30% of people over the age of 60. Without that natural cushion, the bones in your feet come into closer contact with the ground, which causes a deep bruise-like pain in the heels or balls of the feet when walking barefoot or standing for long periods.

For some perspective, look at the doughy wonders that are baby feet and compare them to yours. As we age, wear and tear breaks down that plush tissue. And if you put your feet to heavy use, you’ll wear down that cushion quicker. Some of that internal cushioning can be restored—even if just temporarily—with the injection of dermal fillers.

“It’s getting very popular because people are already familiar with it for aesthetic [uses],” says Ben Pearl, DPM, a podiatrist at Arlington Foot and Ankle in Arlington, Virginia. Dr. Pearl specializes in sports medicine and treats endurance athletes looking to restore cushion lost in their feet from pounding the pavement.

Patients don’t have just one choice for injectables, though. Many of the same options available for cosmetic use have also shown promise for feet. There’s hyaluronic acid filler, which adds physical volume and cushioning, and calcium hydroxylapatite, such as Radiesse, which adds firm volume while also promoting latest collagen growth. Sometimes human body fat is used as the injectable, known as adipose tissue, a practice that is quickly becoming the preferred method.

“[A fat injection] actually recruits your body to rebuild the fat pad in that area so it has a much longer duration,” states Anne Sharkey, DPM, of Soley Podiatry in Austin. Fat allografts from brands like Liposana and Leneva may last as long as two years, compared to hyaluronic acid fillers, which typically need a touch up in six to nine months.

This type of regenerative medicine is appealing to patients. It’s not a promise that the foot will return to its former glory, but that it will be “as close to normal as possible,” indicates Dr. Pearl.

Dr. Sharkey and Dr. Pearl have both seen positive results from their patients. Scientific studies corroborate the efficacy of the treatment as well. One small study looking at patients with metatarsal pain found five patients had no more pain six months post-hyaluronic acid injections, and those who still had pain could wear high heels twice as long as they could before the injections. Another study surveying patients who had been injected with body fat reported that their pain improved by more than 70 percent on average, 20 months post injection.

While there are a growing number of cosmetic clinics offering the procedure, Dr. Pearl cautions against allowing just any injector at it. That’s because injecting filler into feet is a more complex procedure than an aesthetic injection. For one, knowing where to inject requires an understanding of the foot’s pressure points. In his own practice, Dr. Pearl uses ultrasound to help determine where to replace the fat to offload the pain. Additionally, Dr. Pearl notes, the skin is much tougher on the feet than the face, making it a more complicated area to inject.

This is one reason why Dr. Sharkey set up her practice to include a nail salon—combining cosmetology and podiatry. Her patients are already familiar with dermal fillers. Within the attached nail salon you can get manicures, pedicures, ingrown nail treatment, toenail reconstruction, or dermal fillers for feet.

Recent findings suggest that try not to groan, but it depends. The cost of the procedure is influenced by how much filler is injected, and which brand is used. Other factors that affect cost include how your provider bills the procedure, and how much experience they have with dermal filler injections.

For cosmetic use, the American Society of Plastic Surgeons places the average cost of hyaluronic acid filler treatment at $715. They estimate nonhyaluronic acid fillers, including Radiesse, Sculptra, and Liposana to cost $901 on average per treatment. However, the feet will almost certainly require more filler than the face, so you can expect the cost to be higher.

In a recent development, but will insurance cover it? Unlikely. “Even though it isn't technically cosmetic, it may not be considered medically necessary, because these procedures are often considered elective and cosmetic branding has a box drawn around it,” indicates Mark Welter, chief strategy and growth officer at Welter Healthcare Partners, a healthcare business management firm.

If you’re transparent with your provider about any financial concerns you have, they can work with you to find a middle ground between pain relief and high costs. Dr. Sharkey, for example, will often offer her patients more affordable hyaluronic acid fillers as temporary pain relief until they’re ready to dive into a more expensive fat injection.

If injectables aren’t accessible to you, there are other ways to deal with foot pain. Here are some options, most of which require a low financial investment.

A podiatrist can help walk you through any of these options and come up with a plan to minimize your pain.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • With the exhibition, the UK-based collective said it aimed to “explore the transformation of landscape through colour and into colour”.
  • The exhibition was jointly created by the two studios to showcase the fresh pigment, developed by Matter at hand from local waste material, on the miniature buildings made by Assemble.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Daisuke Shima.

Architecture collective Assemble has created small, climbable cedar buildings that “play with scale” to showcase a new pigment, made from industrial waste by design studio Matter at hand, at Tokyo‘s SKAC gallery.

With the exhibition, the UK-based collective said it aimed to “explore the transformation of landscape through colour and into colour”.

The exhibition was jointly created by the two studios to showcase the fresh pigment, developed by Matter at hand from local waste material, on the miniature buildings made by Assemble.

The blue hue was manufactured by Japanese company Nikken to be used in the Play Earth Park – a campsite designed by Assemble that is currently under development in rural Japan.

“The pigment was essentially created by analysing local material waste streams in Toyama and exploring what kind of different colours could be produced from them,” Matter at hand founder Lewis Jones told Dezeen.

“In the end, the blue uses a combination of rice husk ash, limestone filter dust, recycled glass and copper, which are mixed together with water to form a thick clay-like paste and then heated in an electric kiln to around 950ºC,” he continued.

“The materials react to form a fresh crystal phase – known as cuprorivaite, which is bright blue.”.

Recent findings suggest that to show it off, Assemble constructed three miniature houses from Japanese cedar that draw on the agricultural buildings found close to where the pigment material was sourced. The houses were named The Hut, The Tower and The Bird.

“The form of the structures plays with the agricultural buildings within the dispersed settlement of rural Toyama; these buildings evolve over time, adapting to what’s needed, often evolving interesting geometries,” Assemble co-founder Maria Lisogorskaya told Dezeen.

“We tried to play with scale and make the buildings surreal, creating miniature versions of them for play.”.

Sources indicate that the buildings have deliberately simple yet evocative geometries that nod to the structures that inspired them. Among them is a barn-like building surrounded by hay bales.

Assemble’s aim was for visitors to be able to climb and explore the structures.

“We hope that the buildings are climbed on and inhabited; and this exhibition is the beginning of the structures’ life as a play space outside SKWAT,” Lisogorskaya noted.

“The spirit of resourcefulness, fun, and reimagining of our environments is at the core of the project and we look forward to seeing how the structures are used in ways we didn’t expect.”.

The exhibition, which also showcases raw materials used to create the blue colour and products covered in it, is on show in Skwat Kameari Art Centre (SKAC’s) Park gallery in Kameari, Tokyo.

Assemble said it chose to showcase it here as it feels the gallery has a similar spirit to its own UK bases.

“We think SKAC is an amazing interdisciplinary space, and its spirit resonates with how we have set up our studios and labs in London and Liverpool,” Lisogorskaya mentioned.

“Bringing together design, material experimentation with other arts practices as a more satisfying and richer way of being in the city,” she continued.

SKAC recently opened two new gallery spaces, Material Matters (MM) and Space III, as part of a major extension.

The east Tokyo gallery has previously shown exhibitions including anime-informed chairs by Kwangho Lee and reading spaces by Herzog & de Meuron.

According to recent reports, building Blue is at SKAC, 3-26-4 Kameari, Katsushika-ku, Tokyo 125-0002, from 7 November 2026 to 28 February 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Photography by Daisuke Shima.

#125843. What Is ‘Fiber Training’—And Why Should You Be Doing It?

📅 14 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1173 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

What Is ‘Fiber Training’—And Why Should You Be Doing It?

📅 14 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1173 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, with the fibermaxxing fad encouraging people to prioritize this chronically neglected nutrient, one glitch keeps coming up: the side effects.
  • Industry observers note that to be clear, GI distress isn’t a sign to abandon your pursuit of a higher-fiber diet.
  • But if you feel apprehensive at the thought of fighting constant stomach discomfort in the process of working to correct a fiber deficiency, we don’t blame you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, with the fibermaxxing fad encouraging people to prioritize this chronically neglected nutrient, one glitch keeps coming up: the side effects. As important as hitting your daily fiber goal is, your body doesn’t always make doing so easy. Fiber is difficult for your digestive system to break down and has to be handed off to bacteria in the colon instead (which is kind of its point), so piling on too much too fast can result in a barrage of painful, awkward, or inconvenient digestive symptoms—bloating, gas, stomach cramps, the whole nine yards.

Industry observers note that to be clear, GI distress isn’t a sign to abandon your pursuit of a higher-fiber diet. “Even with fiber becoming a growing trend, people still greatly underestimate its importance and, also, just how many ways it benefits the human body,” Desiree Nielsen, RD, a recipe developer with a focus on plant-based nutrition, tells SELF. You’re probably familiar with fiber’s ability to keep you full, stave off constipation, and support gut health, but it wears plenty of other hats too, like lowering “bad” LDL cholesterol and stabilizing your blood sugar (not to mention reducing your risk for a slew of diseases in the long run). In fact, overlooking fiber is one of the top nutrition mistakes people make, according to experts.

But if you feel apprehensive at the thought of fighting constant stomach discomfort in the process of working to correct a fiber deficiency, we don’t blame you. In fact, it’s a complaint that Lisa Ganjhu, DO, a gastroenterologist at NYU Langone Health, hears all the time at work: “I have a lot of patients that will say ‘I ate more fiber, and now I’m really bloated and crampy,’” she claims. Thankfully, there’s a way to curtail those disagreeable side effects so you can (comfortably) continue your fiber journey: a strategy Nielsen calls fiber training. Here’s what that involves, and how to start developing those “muscles.”.

Fiber training is exactly what it sounds like: training your body to handle fiber better. It’s all about “slow, consistent increases in fiber to help you build your tolerance…while minimizing the potential symptoms,” Nielsen says.

You can think of fiber training kind of like preparing for a race. “In much the same way that you wouldn’t go out and run a marathon tomorrow if you haven’t run a mile before,” you need to work your way up to a high-fiber diet, Nielsen states. Similarly, Dr. Ganjhu compares it to a weightlifting regimen. Rather than lifting 50-pound weights right off the bat, “you kind of have to adjust slowly,” she says. “You start off with 10. When that becomes easy, you go to 20, then you go to 30”—and so on.

Industry observers note that fiber training is especially critical if you’re constipated at the outset, as many people are, according to Nielsen. Even though fiber can help prevent and alleviate constipation, too much at once can actually make an existing issue worse by overwhelming your gut. “When you add a ton of fiber to an already backed-up system, it’s kind of like a bottleneck on the highway,” Nielsen notes: If you try to shoehorn four lanes into one, you’re going to end up with a jam on your hands.

Now that you know fiber training entails steadily increasing your fiber intake, you’re probably wondering what that looks like on a more practical level. Before we share specifics, some context for how much fiber you actually need might be helpful. Per the federal Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020-2025, women should aim for 28 grams of fiber daily from ages 19 to 30, 25 grams of fiber daily from ages 31 to 50, and 22 grams of fiber daily starting at age 51, though some experts recommend even more—a helpful set of parameters if you’re not sure where to start.

While the ideal amount of fiber to add to your diet while fiber training can vary from person to person depending on health needs (like a constipation problem), most people are “looking at [adding] probably three to five grams at a time,” Nielsen states.

Recent findings suggest that with that in mind, you’ll want to choose a food that has a fiber content in that ballpark—say, an apple (around four grams of fiber), a half-cup of chickpeas (around five grams of fiber), a tablespoon of chia seeds (around five grams of fiber), or two tablespoons of ground flax (around four grams of fiber)—and eat a serving every single day until you feel like your body has adjusted (read: you’re not experiencing any additional bloating, gas, or other GI side effects). This process typically takes around five to seven days, according to Nielsen, but everyone’s digestive system is different, so don’t worry if you need more (or less!) time. “It really is about listening to your body and individualizing the rate at which you increase,” Nielsen claims. “You have to follow your symptoms and go slow,” Dr. Ganjhu agrees.

Industry observers note that then, you can tack on another dose—like a second apple, a full cup of chickpeas, two tablespoons of chia seeds, or four tablespoons of ground flax. Continue increasing your fiber intake in these increments (and at this pace) until you’ve hit your daily fiber goal. If you’re a 35-year-old woman starting from scratch, reaching 25 grams of fiber—the recommended daily amount for that age—would take around five five-gram doses, six four-gram doses, or eight three-gram doses, for example.

People who are constipated may want to specifically fiber train with foods that are low in FODMAPs—fermentable carbohydrates particularly hard on sensitive stomachs—according to Nielsen. Like we said above, increasing your fiber intake when you’re backed up can, well, backfire, so low-FODMAP foods are more likely to be a safe bet than their high-FODMAP counterparts. Kiwis, which contain four grams of fiber in a two-fruit serving, are an especially strong option if you fall into this category (and they’ve even been specifically studied as a dietary constipation treatment), Nielsen notes. Similarly, she adds, a gentle fiber supplement like Metamucil, which is made from psyllium husk, also “provides a lot of the benefits, but tends to be less irritating to a troubled system.”.

Another tip: If you’re constipated, make sure to drink plenty of water as well (though the oft-referenced eight-glasses-a-day requirement is something of a myth!). Because fiber needs water to work its stool-softening magic, insufficient fluids could leave your bowel movements hard and dry, exacerbating the problem.

Whatever new fiber sources you choose, taking this slow-and-steady approach should help ease the transition to a higher intake. “If you’re someone who doesn’t eat a lot of fiber and all of a sudden you start eating 30 grams of it, the colon is just not going to know how to manage that efficiently,” Dr. Ganjhu says. But by leveling up little by little? You can heighten that “colonic fitness”—and sidestep the worst of the awkward stage.

Photo by Colin Hattersley.

Over one hundred staff at Edinburgh College of Art have signed an open letter addressed to the university, calling on the institution to reverse its decision to cut three craft-focussed design courses from its programme.

Open letter states “deep concern”.

The open letter was signed by 109 unnamed staff members of Edinburgh College of Art, which announced on 15 September that it would stop admitting students for its undergraduate courses in jewellery and silversmithing, textiles and performance costume from 2027.

The move is part of a wider decision by the University of Edinburgh, which the art college merged with in 2011, to make £140 million’s worth of cuts to arts and humanities courses.

“We the undersigned are writing to mark our deep concern about the University of Edinburgh’s current financially-driven restructuring,” states the letter, which was written by an unnamed senior lecturer in the school of design and published yesterday.

“As staff who collectively provide and deliver the teaching, research, technical expertise and administration of design, we assert that there is irreparable harm being done to the core values of our subject area, school, and to the art, craft and design professions in Scotland at large,” it continues.

The open letter also asks the university to retract its decision to close the courses and requests better communication between the university and its employees.

Signatories describe an “alienating” period during which the decision to close the courses was “made without prior consultation with [the university] staff”.

“Rash decision-making based on unsubstantiated and opaque data seems to be characterising the announcements of closures and cuts, and there has been no dialogue with students and staff that can be understood as meaningful or considered consultation,” they state.

“We feel that the area’s staff have been treated callously or with very little regard by senior management, and we are writing, in part, to warn you of the damage this has created and ask you to make effort to repair it.”.

Courses part of “wider ecosystem”.

The letter goes on to emphasise the importance of “individual programmes as valuable parts of [a] wider ecosystem”, and particularly stresses the urgency of craft-based undergraduate courses in the creative sphere.

“Looking specifically at jewellery and silversmithing, textiles, and performance costume, these are subjects that teach, in different and inherently valuable ways, specialised material knowledge and sensibilities, innovative critiques, and developments of systems of production and consumption, great capacities to research-through-making, and the ability to speak to a society’s needs through aesthetic form, the power of narrative, and the arts of material, chemical and technological mastery and manipulation,” it states.

The letter is addressed to the University of Edinburgh Court, the university’s governing body, which is scheduled to meet on 7 December to review the decision.

Sources indicate that the open letter is the most recent statement issued by a collective against the decision to cut the courses. It follows a live petition led by arts organisation Craft Scotland calling for the urgent reinstatement of “the only undergraduate craft courses offered by Edinburgh College of Art” amidst public backlash.

Dezeen has approached Edinburgh College of Art for comment.

Photo by Colin Hattersley.

Why Are People Taking CoQ10 Supplements for Longevity, and Do They Work?

📅 14 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, was once a niche supplement, known best in wellness circles for its possible benefits for heart health and fertility.
  • Industry observers note that the appeal of CoQ10 has grown as researchers have explored its effects on various conditions, with small studies revealing, for example, it may help boost insulin sensitivity, cut the frequency of migraine attacks, and alleviate muscle aches from statins used for high cholesterol.
  • According to recent reports, that role has punched CoQ10’s ticket into the longevity club, alongside other supplements thought to lend a hand to mitochondria (like urolithin A and nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, was once a niche supplement, known best in wellness circles for its possible benefits for heart health and fertility. But now the antioxidant’s star is rising for a latest reason: its purported longevity-boosting powers.

Industry observers note that the appeal of CoQ10 has grown as researchers have explored its effects on various conditions, with small studies revealing, for example, it may help boost insulin sensitivity, cut the frequency of migraine attacks, and alleviate muscle aches from statins used for high cholesterol. But as of late, there’s excitement around its broader anti-aging potential because of how it supports our mitochondria, which you may remember from high school biology as the “powerhouse of the cell.”.

According to recent reports, that role has punched CoQ10’s ticket into the longevity club, alongside other supplements thought to lend a hand to mitochondria (like urolithin A and nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN). There’s even a synthetic derivative of CoQ10 designed specifically for better absorption by mitochondria, which is called mitoquinone (or MitoQ), that’s gaining hype among celeb trainers and athletes for boosting energy, recovery, and “cellular health.”.

According to recent reports, but is CoQ10 all it’s cracked up to be when it comes to longevity? Read on to learn more before grabbing a bottle of this supplement.

Industry observers note that our cells naturally produce CoQ10, a molecule that acts like a conveyor belt for charged particles inside our mitochondria, enabling them to “efficiently create adenosine triphosphate, or ATP,” the “currency for cellular energy,” Anthony Molina, PhD, a professor of medicine at UC San Diego who studies aging biomarkers, tells SELF. That’s a major deal, as all cells rely on that energy to complete their daily functions. As we age, both the number and energy-producing powers of mitochondria drop off—a process involved in the development of many age-related diseases, Dr. Molina points out. Meanwhile, CoQ10 levels also decline with age, leading to the idea that we should take it in supplement form for better mitochondrial (and, in turn, overall) health.

It has been revealed that beyond its role in energy production, CoQ10 is also an antioxidant that is “very powerful in capturing free radicals,” or volatile molecules that can harm cells, Daria Mochly-Rosen, PhD, a professor of chemical and systems biology at Stanford University and coauthor of The Life Machines: How Taking Care of Your Mitochondria Can Transform Your Health, tells SELF. By stabilizing those molecules, CoQ10 may help to keep that damage (a.k.a. oxidative stress) from piling up and also contributing to aging and the development of chronic disease.

Separately, CoQ10 has potential benefits as it relates to cardiovascular health: It’s anti-inflammatory and may also improve the function of blood vessels, helping regulate blood pressure, JoAnn E. Manson, MD, DrPH, chief of the division of preventive medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School, tells SELF. These upsides could lower risk for heart disease, the number-one killer in the US.

Recent findings suggest that despite the promising mechanisms above, “the evidence base just isn’t yet there,” Dr. Manson says. The studies we do have on CoQ10 and longevity are in mice and rats—and while a few suggest a lifespan-extending effect, or a way to reverse some cognitive decline once it starts, others show no anti-aging upsides in healthy animals. Besides, “we find again and again that humans are not just large, non-hairy mice,” Dr. Mochly-Rosen points out, “so we can’t assume the results transfer.”.

Studies in people have been focused on CoQ10 as an intervention for specific diseases, particularly cardiovascular ones. All the experts say the strongest evidence for longevity is in those with heart failure, who have low CoQ10 levels—taking the supplement alongside standard treatment has been shown to reduce the need for hospitalization and risk of early death, possibly because of its mitochondrial perks.

But logistically, it’s a lot trickier to prove that CoQ10 prolongs life in healthy people versus in those with a medical condition or known CoQ10 deficiency. In the absence of these studies, it might be tempting to take a logical leap: If we know CoQ10 supports mitochondrial function, and levels of both dip with age and disease, supplementing with CoQ10 seems like it should help you live longer. But the problem is, we don’t know exactly what drives the mitochondrial challenges that occur with age, Dr. Molina says. “So maybe you’re not taking a shot in the dark because we know that mitochondria has something to do with healthy aging, but using CoQ10 as the tool is like taking a shot in a dimly lit room,” he says. “It’s not clear whether you’re hitting the right target.”.

According to recent reports, as with any supplement, it’s best to ask your doctor before adding CoQ10 to your routine. While there’s a good deal of data to suggest it’s safe and well-tolerated, there are some people who shouldn’t take it, generally because of interactions with prescription drugs, Dr. Molina points out. The main concern is with blood thinners (a.k.a. anticoagulants) like warfarin (which are often prescribed after a blood clot)—CoQ10 could make these drugs less effective, Dr. Manson states. It’s also extra crucial to check in with your doctor first if you take insulin or are receiving treatment for cancer. Though CoQ10 doesn’t usually cause side effects, you could also wind up with some mild GI upset or insomnia, Dr. Manson adds.

Recent findings suggest that there’s also the quality-control problem that comes with any supplement. These are not subjected to the same FDA regulations as medications are, meaning you can’t know for sure that you’re getting what the bottle promises. Studies of certain CoQ10 supplements have found that they contained less of the antioxidant than the amount listed on the label, Dr. Mochly-Rosen notes. Your best defense against winding up with a sugar pill is to find a product that’s been third-party verified, she states—look for the “NSF certified” or “USP verified” stamp.

Though it’s been used as a natural remedy for centuries, jojoba oil is having a major hair moment right now.

Keep reading to learn how to use it for strong, shiny hair and a healthy scalp.

Recent findings suggest that “Jojoba oil is incredibly nourishing,” claims Mayara Macedo, a hairstylist and scalp specialist in NYC. “It’s a natural oil that closely resembles the sebum our skin and scalp produce,” Macedo explains.

Because of this, Macedo says it’s super compatible with our bodies and works great as a balancing treatment — whether you have an oily or dry scalp.

While its proven benefits mainly revolve around its help with scalp health, jojoba oil can also strengthen and moisturize hair. However, it’s not the go-to pick for improving hair loss (that’s usually minoxidil).

If you’re dealing with dryness, jojoba oil is fantastic for adding moisture to your scalp,” Macedo says.

“Its natural hydrating properties help restore balance, leaving everything healthier and more manageable.”.

“Jojoba oil has been known for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties in addition to its conditioning and emollient properties,” indicates Kseniya Kobets, MD, board-certified dermatologist and Director of Cosmetics Dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care.

These properties help out with dry, irritating dandruff.

This also explains jojoba oil‘s Mexican Indian history as a treatment for sores, which eventually caused researchers to flag its potential for improving skin conditions like acne and psoriasis (but please see a dermatologist for proven treatment options).

Though many say that jojoba oil grows hair, this claim is probably tossed around because it helps moisturize hair follicles — which can keep dryness at bay.

A dry environment can be a breeding ground for breakage, hair loss, and dandruff.

Also, your split ends say hello — jojoba oil can help by restoring hair health overall.

“If your scalp gets oily quickly after washing,” Macedo indicates, “It could be because your scalp is overcompensating, thinking it doesn’t have enough moisture and needs to produce more oil.”.

She indicates adding jojoba oil helps signal to your scalp that it has enough, which can slow down excess oil production.

Although you can apply jojoba oil to the length and tips of your hair, Macedo says she prefers to use it only for the scalp, saying that other oils, like argan oil, will work better for the length.

You can also buy shampoos or conditions that already have it!

Macedo says you can apply jojoba oil to wet or dry hair, depending on your goal.

“Applying it to dry hair reduces frizz and adds a light shine to styled hair,” she suggests.

Kobets recommends using oils overnight for extended exposure. However, she points out this can get messy (RIP pillowcases), so you can always apply them for a few hours and wash them off before bed.

According to recent reports, macedo also suggests being mindful of the amount you use — too much can make your hair look greasy, especially true for fine hair. “For a lightweight finish, start with a small amount and focus on the ends of your hair. But again, I’d recommend jojoba oil for the scalp and argan oil for the hair,” Macedo adds.

“If you’re using jojoba oil as a pre-wash treatment to balance scalp oil or as a deep conditioner, apply it before washing,” Macedo explains. “If you’re using it as a leave-in conditioner or frizz-tamer, you can apply it to freshly washed hair — careful not to apply too much.”.

Kobets suggests washing the scalp after using oils, noting that her patients don’t always prefer to use them because they can reduce hair volume for some.

It’s not the move for improving hair loss, however.

#125837. Tech Report: Are trees on buildings more than a greenwashing gimmick?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1715 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dezeen ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Are trees on buildings more than a greenwashing gimmick?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For more than a decade, buildings bearing trees have been sprouting up all over the world, from Newly introduced York to Paris to Shanghai to Sydney.
  • It has arguably become one of the defining architectural trends of our era, taken up enthusiastically by top studios including SIGNIFICANT, MVRDV, MAD and Ateliers Jean Nouvel.
  • Recent findings suggest that and yet, not everyone is a fan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Main photo by Dimitar Harizanov.

For more than a decade, buildings bearing trees have been sprouting up all over the world, from Newly introduced York to Paris to Shanghai to Sydney.

It has arguably become one of the defining architectural trends of our era, taken up enthusiastically by top studios including SIGNIFICANT, MVRDV, MAD and Ateliers Jean Nouvel.

Recent findings suggest that and yet, not everyone is a fan. Almost every time Dezeen publishes an arboreal structure, a volley of comments crying greenwashing and gimmickry soon follows.

So, are the haters right on this one? Or do the arguments stack up in favour of wooded buildings?

To proponents of the approach, some of the benefits of putting trees on buildings are indisputable.

“I’m totally in favor of not only trees on buildings, but any type of natural habitats on buildings wherever it’s possible,” stated Fernando Scherner, an associate director in the nature and biodiversity team at engineering firm Buro Happold. “There are a few things that I think we can’t even argue about anymore.”.

There is, Scherner told Dezeen, strong evidence that vegetation on buildings bolsters biodiversity. And, he says, “there’s no discussion” that done right, shade and evapotranspiration from leaves can effectively keep homes cooler in hot weather, reducing the need for air conditioning – and therefore energy use.

But this second point gestures towards the crux of the debate about trees on buildings.

Sources indicate that such buildings require extra structural material to support the weight of the trees and soil, increasing the carbon cost by more than what the trees themselves will be able to sequester. Critics therefore argue that any carbon savings from reduced energy use are a red herring, because a similar benefit could be achieved through much simpler passive cooling measures such as awnings and shutters.

“I think that criticism is entirely legitimate, particularly if carbon sequestration is being used as the main justification,” stated World Green Building Council technical lead for sustainable buildings Carolina Montano Owen.

“Trees do sequester carbon, but relatively slowly compared with the upfront emissions that can arise from additional reinforced concrete or steel needed for large planters, supporting structure and associated systems.”.

Even Dutch architecture studio MVRDV, one of the most fervent incorporators of trees on buildings, admitted in its Carbon Confessions exhibition held earlier this year that it would take hundreds of years to offset the climate impact of its La Serre project in Paris, currently under construction. MVRDV declined to contribute to this article.

While the phenomenon of trees on buildings goes back hundreds of years, to the Guinigi Tower in Tuscany, the undisputed poster child for the current movement stands at the other end of Italy.

Bosco Verticale in Milan is a pair of residential high-rises covered in 21,000 plants, including 800 trees up to 20 metres tall. It caused a sensation upon its completion in 2014, and was later selected by Dezeen as that year’s most significant building in the world.

The architect behind Bosco Verticale, Stefano Boeri, has since delivered other “vertical forests” in Eindhoven, Huanggang, Tirana and Utrecht, with several more on the way.

According to recent reports, as you’d expect, he is bullish about the benefits of putting trees on buildings. He points to analysis by Arup, which concluded that the embodied carbon of Bosco Verticale is just one per cent greater than a comparable building with balconies of the same depth without vegetation.

“The load of the greenery, including the soil, trees and so on, really only slightly exceeds the variable loads that, in any case, must necessarily be taken into account in the structural design of cantilevered space,” he told Dezeen.

Boeri argues that changes to the construction process – such as the use of prefabrication methods or mass timber – promise to cut the embodied cost further in future vertical forest projects.

Even so, Philip Oldfield, head of the University of New South Wales’ School of Built Environment, is not convinced.

“I think the equation is pretty challenging to make the case that trees on buildings are beneficial from a greenhouse-gas emissions perspective,” he told Dezeen.

However, Oldfield points out, that’s not to say that architects adorning their buildings with trees are necessarily acting in bad faith.

According to recent reports, “I’m a fan of Bosco Verticale,” he remarked. “I think it’s a really inspiring building, but not from a carbon perspective.”.

“What inspires me about Bosco Verticale is it claims, ‘hey, look: you can have a hint of suburban lifestyle in a high-rise urban building,’ which could make high-density living more attractive to a greater socio-economic spectrum, and then that may be more sustainable in the long run.”.

Though harder to measure than carbon, it’s generally acknowledged that incorporating greenery into dense urban settings has positives for human wellbeing.

For instance, when Oldfield helped to conduct a post-occupancy study of the social housing development Pinnacle@Duxton in Singapore, he witnessed children sitting under trees to do their homework 50 storeys in the sky.

“Singapore’s been able to add trees and green across its built environment, and it has fundamentally changed the experience of the city, I think for the better,” he said.

With a very high-rise urban landscape, year-round hot weather, lots of rain and low wind speeds, Singapore is the perfect setting for buildings bearing trees, and the construction industry here has become adept at making it work.

According to recent reports, but in other parts of the world, things have gone less successfully. Jean Nouvel’s One Central Park in Sydney, for example, had to undergo emergency repairs after one of its heavy planter boxes fell to the ground in 2022.

And in Chengdu, there were reports that barely any of the 826 apartments at Qiyi City Forest Garden were occupied a few years after its completion due to a mosquito infestation.

Even the most ardent fans of trees on buildings agree that it’s not always the right solution.

According to recent reports, “I’m totally positive about it, but I think it should be taken case-by-case,” said Scherner. “There may be cases where the purpose or the objective of the project are not really realistic.”.

“If the right multidisciplinary team is not there from the start – and I’m talking about ecologists, horticulturalists, together with engineers, structural engineers, architects, landscape architects and all that – then many things can go wrong.”.

Sources indicate that “There are many flops,” remarked Boeri. “If you decide to follow the approach that we have, you take several risks, so it’s very important to be aware of the risk and to run all the technical challenges and tools that you need if you want to do it properly.”.

“Botany is not a superficial discipline – it’s very complex, very rich, and so when you want to realise a building where trees are acting as live subjects, you have to study a lot.”.

Bosco Verticale was subject to a huge amount of strategic planning in collaboration with botanists, from the selection and preparation of the plants, to soil chemistry, to developing systems for irrigation and maintenance.

“Flying gardeners” now scale the buildings twice a year, while thousands of ladybirds were purchased to control pests and cranes were installed on top of the towers in anticipation of removing larger dead trees. In the event, Boeri claims fewer than 15 trees have died at Bosco Verticale, and the cranes have never been required.

Sceptics’ early predictions of mass plant deaths at buildings bearing trees have, in general, not come to pass.

But concern about whether some of these buildings are more interested in making a visual statement than being ecologically responsible has lingered.

For Montano Owen, this is the crucial test of whether the approach is justified.

“The difference is whether planting is an integrated environmental strategy or primarily aesthetic,” she noted.

“A poor example is essentially decorative: oversized concrete or steel planters added to achieve a ‘green’ aesthetic, substantial additional structural loads, high irrigation requirements, inappropriate species, difficult maintenance access and high tree mortality.”.

Boeri agrees. “I believe that what we have done works because we were not considering plants as an ornamental presence, and this is very important for me,” he said. “What we are doing is really to create buildings for trees, a house for trees.”.

Among the most high-profile projects accused of using trees as mere decoration is Heatherwick Studio’s 1,000 Trees shopping centre in Shanghai, completed in 2022.

Soon after the finished building was unveiled, Oldfield criticised the design in a piece on Dezeen.

“The trees are a one-liner, contributing to a sense of urban drama, but with little substance as to how they might provide tangible benefits to the environment, or the community,” he wrote.

According to recent reports, subject to similar criticisms recently was MVRDV’s design for the upcoming Rotterdam Rocks!. Writing on Dezeen, architecture historian Barnabas Calder called for the project to be scrapped, saying that “putting plants on a building doesn’t make it sustainable, any more than dropping a basil leaf on a steak makes it vegan”.

These studios may argue – as Heatherwick Studio leader Thomas Heatherwick has previously done – that there is intrinsic value in designing buildings that capture the imagination of the public.

That in turn feeds into a broader debate about whether the priority for architecture should be to minimise up-front carbon, or maximise the chance that buildings are retained by future generations.

In any case, with the trees-on-buildings trend showing little sign of abating, Montano Owen has a checklist for architects taking up the approach.

In a recent development, “Start with the local context and environmental needs,” she noted. “Choose species that are suited to the location. Minimise extra structure, materials and loads. Consider water and maintenance needs from the start. Plan for vegetation to survive, grow and mature long term. Avoid solutions that need heavy structures, intensive irrigation or frequent plant replacement for limited environmental benefit.”.

In a recent development, “The key question is this,” she added. “Is this the best place and most resource-efficient way to achieve the environmental benefits we want? Sometimes trees on buildings could make sense. In most cases, trees at street or ground level may provide greater benefits with fewer resources.”.

Everyone Wants This Unapproved Weight Loss Drug—And Some Have Found a Way to Get It

📅 14 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for all the hype surrounding GLP-1 weight loss medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, these drugs don’t work for everyone.
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s called retatrutide, and it’s a triple-agonist medication, which means it acts on three different receptors in the body.
  • Retatrutide is already being hailed as a game changer in an area of health that’s already welcomed plenty of impressive medications in the past few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for all the hype surrounding GLP-1 weight loss medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, these drugs don’t work for everyone. Nearly 17% of people on these medications are considered “non-responders,” leaving them looking for a different solution. But there’s a buzzy new medication waiting in the wings. While it’s not yet approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), people are already seeking it out.

Recent findings suggest that it’s called retatrutide, and it’s a triple-agonist medication, which means it acts on three different receptors in the body. By comparison, Wegovy (semaglutide) acts on one receptor, while Zepbound (tirzepatide) works on two.

Retatrutide is already being hailed as a game changer in an area of health that’s already welcomed plenty of impressive medications in the past few years. In fact, clinical trial results show that it’s so effective for weight loss that some people have dropped out of the trials because they felt that they lost too much weight.

But retatrutide is still being tested in clinical trials. Eli Lilly, which makes reatrutide and Zepbound, hasn’t even submitted the trial results yet to the FDA for approval. So this is still an experimental medication—and versions of it are being sold online for cheap.

In a recent development, mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California, tells SELF that retatrutide is “not really available” for use just yet, short of signing up for a clinical trial. There is no set timeline for when it will hit the market, given that clinical trial results have not yet been submitted to the FDA.

In a recent development, if you’ve struggled with losing weight on a GLP-1 medication or just want to pay significantly less for what appears to be the next big thing in weight loss drugs, it’s understandable to be tempted to add this to your cart. Here’s why doctors recommend resisting the urge.

Industry observers note that retatrutide is similar to GLP-1 medications in a few ways. Namely, it’s used for weight loss and is given once a week through an injection. Like Wegovy, Ozempic, and Zepbound, retatrutide works by reducing appetite and slowing digestion.

Sources indicate that but retatrutide has more going on than that. This medication acts on three hormone receptors in the body—glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP), and glucagon (GCG). “This is the first one in the pipeline to work on three different receptors,” says Dr. Ali. “The theory is that the more receptors it affects, the more effective the drug will be.”.

Recent findings suggest that the medication is currently in phase-three clinical trials, and it’s had some impressive results that suggest it could be the most effective drug for weight loss yet. The latest clinical trial results show that participants lost an average of 28.7% of their body weight on the highest dose of retatrutide over 68 weeks. By comparison, tirzepatide customers lost an average of 15% to 22.5% over 72 weeks during clinical trials, and semaglutide users lost 10% to 15% of their body weight over 68 weeks during clinical trials.

It takes a little detective work, but there are some pharmacies that are selling the drug online.

In fact, this has become such an matter that the FDA issued a press release in early February, stressing that it’s illegal to sell retatrutide (and fellow experimental weight loss medication cagrilintide) right now. That includes picking up the medication from a compounding pharmacy.

It has been revealed that “Retatrutide and cagrilintide cannot be used in compounding under federal law,” the release states. “Additionally, these are not components of FDA-approved drugs and have not been found safe and effective for any condition.”.

The FDA also noted that its officials have issued warning letters to companies that are distributing these medications.

This is hardly shocking, but doctors really want you to take a pass on using retatrutide before it’s FDA-approved.

It has been revealed that “People should wait to take medications until they are approved by the FDA to maximize safety,” Richard Siegel, MD, codirector of the Diabetes and Lipid Center at Tufts Medical Center and endocrinologist at Tufts Medicine Weight & Wellness Center–Stoneham, tells SELF. “All scientific data in animals initially and then humans are carefully reviewed by the FDA for any signals that a medication may be harmful.”.

It has been revealed that that includes side effects you might experience now or in the future, Dr. Ali points out. Compounding pharmacies have become a gray area. They’re able to legally produce and sell their own versions of popular medications when the FDA-approved versions are in shortage. But technically this is no longer legal once the medications are out of shortage.

Industry observers note that but compounded drugs aren’t carefully regulated and may not even have the same ingredients or concentration as the medication they’re designed to mimic, Dr. Siegel indicates. “While these medications may be safe, there is less oversight in their production,” he says.

Dr. Ali warns against going directly through a compounding pharmacy, noting that it’s safer to work with your health care provider if you strategy to go this route. “The worst-case scenario is that you’re getting something unsafe or ineffective,” he notes.

It has been revealed that but, with all medications, Dr. Ali says it’s best to use the FDA-approved version whenever possible. “It’s going to work in a predictable way, and the side effect profile will be well-studied,” he says.

According to recent reports, dr. Siegel points out that there are a lot of options to lose weight right now. And, if you haven’t had success on one, he recommends talking to your healthcare provider about trying a different medication or strategy. If you haven’t had luck while working with a primary care physician, Dr. Ali suggests seeing an obesity medicine specialist who will be more knowledgeable about treatment options.

According to recent reports, “Medications for weight management are a powerful tool that should be used together with a comprehensive lifestyle blueprint focusing on self-monitoring, optimal nutrition, and an exercise prescription, including both aerobic and resistance components,” Dr. Siegel says. Meaning, people who have the best results do more than take medication—they also focus on nutrition and exercise.

According to recent reports, if you’re interested in taking a weight loss medication or your existing treatment isn’t working, talk to a healthcare provider who specializes in this area. “These medications are designed for people with significant weight to lose,” Dr. Ali says. “Most likely, they will need to be taken long-term.” That makes getting a well-vetted medication from a reputable source even more important, he points out.

Five key projects by Dezeen Awards emerging designer of the year Simon Skinner

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Peter Hansen unless stated.
  • This year Simon Skinner was named emerging designer of the year at the Dezeen Awards.
  • Swedish designer Skinner set up his studio in 2020 and has rapidly become known for his sculptural furniture and installations that explore rethinking and reusing found materials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Peter Hansen unless stated.

This year Simon Skinner was named emerging designer of the year at the Dezeen Awards. Here, he selects five projects that showcase his work.

Swedish designer Skinner set up his studio in 2020 and has rapidly become known for his sculptural furniture and installations that explore rethinking and reusing found materials.

“My practice is centred around material culture, exploring the relationship between objects, meaning and everyday life,” Skinner told Dezeen.

“What connects my work is an interest in how forms carry associations and how these can be reshaped to offer upcoming perspectives on things we know and take for granted.”.

Skinner finds that the things that excite him about design are also “the same things that make me suffer”.

“You never quite know what’s coming next when running your own practice, but there’s also something exciting about that uncertainty,” he remarked.

“A material or an object you’ve overlooked for years can suddenly become the starting point for a whole body of work.”.

Over the coming year, along with creating new collections and public installations, Skinner hopes to dedicate more time to research.

“I want to make more room for research and experimentation, and give myself time to follow an interest before knowing exactly where it might lead,” he said.

Sources indicate that “When I started researching Afro combs at Konstfack, I became aware of how much history and symbolism an everyday tool can hold. That experience still informs how I work,” he continued.

“I want to keep exploring the objects and forms we take for granted, looking at the meanings they’ve inherited and what happens when you change their material, scale or context.”.

Read on to find out five key projects by Dezeen Award-winning Skinner, as described by the designer:.

“An ongoing project in which vintage glass sourced from flea markets and second-hand shops is brought together in sculptural lighting compositions.

“Drawing on the memories and associations embedded in these found objects, the work explores the relationship between material, memory and light.”.

“Crafted in my studio, these combs celebrate rituals and traditions surrounding textured hair.

“Informed by historical references and personal experiences, they reimagine an everyday object through distinctive forms and symbols.”.

“Extending the exploration of beauty rituals within the Syntax collection, the Vanity Table offers an alternative reading of an object associated with personal grooming.”.

“These one-of-a-kind pieces, a daybed and an armchair, are upholstered in hand-dyed canvas in deep magenta hues.

“Combining traditional upholstery techniques with an experimental approach to colour and detail, the pieces embrace the irregularities of the dyeing process, making them an integral part of their character.”.

It has been revealed that “This piece of furniture explores our relationship to the mechanical lock. The lock is integrated into the leg, with keys used to secure the connection between the leg and the seat.

Meet Laerke Ryom, Patricia Urquiola's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years
